text: Introduction
Elbow dislocation is the second most common large joint dislocation in adults (up to 25%) and the most common large joint dislocation in children
It mostly affect younger patients aged 10-20 years due to sports injuries and high energy injuries (e.g. road traffic accidents)
That is because, the elbow is a highly stable joint, it requires a considerable amount of force to be dislocated
Anatomy
Elbow is a hinge type of synovial joint
It is formed by the articulation of the capitulum and trochlea of the distal humerus with the radial head and trochlear notch of the radius and ulna respectively.
The articular surfaces of these bones are almost in full contact with each other leading to higher stability of the elbow joint
DrJanaOfficial, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Anatomy
The joint capsule of the elbow surrounds the elbow joint and provide more stability
Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Anatomy
Elbow joint is furtherly stabilized by ligaments, those include:
radial collateral ligament: connect lateral epicondyle of the humerus with the annular ligament
Annular ligament of the radius: encircles the radial head into the ulnar notch
Ulnar collateral ligament: connects medial epicondyle of the humerus to the coronoid process and olecranon of the ulna and it contain two bands anterior and posterior
Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Anatomy
Muscles around the elbow joint also help in stabilization (common flexors, common extensors, brachialis, triceps …)
All of these factors make the elbow a highly stable joint but sometimes dislocation occur
InjuryMap, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Pathological anatomy
When elbow dislocation occurs, this may lead to:
Bony injury (radial head fracture, coronoid process fracture)
Capsular injury
Ligament injury (especially medial collateral ligament)
Muscle injury
In simple dislocations, there will be no bone injury but the capsule and ligaments will be injured, however the elbow will be reduced and it will still be stable after reduction
Pathological anatomy

In complex elbow dislocations, there will be bone injury in association with the capsular and ligamentous injuries; radial head being the most common associated fracture and coronoid process of the ulna being second most common, in these injuries were there is elbow dislocation and only one fracture (either radial head or coronoid process) then elbow will also be stable after reduction in most cases

If all of these three come together (elbow dislocation + radial head fracture + coronoid process fracture) then this is called terrible triad injury and in this case elbow will be unstable after reduction with bad prognosis (recurrent dislocations and osteoarthiritis)
Classification
Elbow dislocations are classified according to the direction of displacement of the forearm relative to the arm into posterior (90%), anterior, medial, lateral and convergent
Elbow dislocations also classified into simple and complex, simple is without associated fracture and complex is with associated fractures (e.g. coronoid process fracture or radial head fracture)
Hipnotic88, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Coronoid process fracture classification
Ulnar coronoid process is classified according to Regan and Morrey classification
Regan and Morrey classifies coronoid process fractures according to the size of the fractured fragment into:
Type I: fracture of the tip of the coronoid process (small fragment)
Type II: fracture of < 50% coronoid process fragment
Type III: fracture of > 50% coronoid process fragment
Palica assumed (based on copyright claims)., CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
Symptoms
Patient present with elbow pain and deformity, patient elbow is usually held in slight flexion and supported by the other hand
Clinical features
Physical examination
Look
Elbow swelling
There might be ecchymosis around the elbow
Deformity is obvious
Feel
there is tenderness on pressure around the elbow, and bony landmarks (olecranon and epicondyles) maybe abnormally placed
Check radial pulse and compare with other hand to make sure no vascular injury is sustained
Neurological examination will reveal Ulnar nerve injury in most cases
Clinical features
Move
Patient refuse to move their elbow
Imaging
Plain radiographs are enough for diagnosis, CT scan maybe required for surgical planning and assessment
AP and lateral elbow x rays shows the dislocation well, radiocapitellar line is drawn to make it easier to spot the dislocation
The challenge with plain radiographs is to identify the associated injuries
Tracy Kilborn, Halvani Moodley and Stewart MearsAdded annotations: Mikael Häggström, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons
Imaging
The dislocation direction is described, also the associated fractures and injuries should also be described in the report
In the x ray, the dislocation is divergent, in which there is ulnohumeral, radiohumeral and proximal radioulnar joints all dislocated
Article authors: Tracy Kilborn, Halvani Moodley and Stewart MearsAdded annotations: Mikael Häggström, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Associated injuries
Radial head fracture
Coronoid process fracture
Terrible triad injury
Medial epicondyle fracture (mostly in children)
Treatment
Simple elbow dislocations are treated non operatively with closed reduction
Elbow closed reduction maneuver 1:
Patient is placed supine and procedural sedation is usually required
Ask an assistant to provide counter traction at the proximal humerus
Patient wrist is held with one hand while the dislocated elbow is manipulated from the underside by the other hand
Reduce any medial/ lateral displacement first by the hand under the elbow
Then apply traction using both hands with flexion of patient elbow to 90 degrees
Treatment
Elbow closed reduction maneuver 2:
Ask assistant to hold patient wrist and apply traction with flexion
You hold and push the olecranon distally, anteriorly and medially using your thumbs
Reduction is confirmed by assessing the full range of motion and varus and valgus stress application while doing that
After that, the elbow is immobilized in above elbow backslab with 90 degrees of flexion for 1 week and then exercises started
Treatment
Repeat radiographs to make sure reduction is good and joint is congruent (joint space equal along the articular surfaces) and repeat neuro examination
Indications of operative treatment
Failure of closed reduction
Joint instability
Complex fracture dislocations => requires reduction and management of the fractures and damaged soft tissues
Operative management of elbow injuries usually carries poor prognosis due to secondary osteoarthritis
Complications
Nerve injury
Ulnar nerve: most common to be injured with posterior dislocations (neuropraxia)
Median nerve: maybe entrapped during closed reduction of posterior dislocations
Radial nerve
Complications
Brachial artery: with anterior dislocations => requires emergency surgery to repair the artery
Stiffness: loss of 20-30 degrees of terminal extension of the elbow due to prolonged immobilization
Heterotopic ossification: lead to more stiffness
Complications
Recurrent dislocation: most commonly caused by radial collateral ligament incompetence and fracture dislocation
Secondary osteoarthritis

text: Introduction
Radial and Ulna shaft fractures occur commonly
The radius and ulna are linked together, so they get fractured together in most cases. But a fracture to a single bone can occur in some cases
Most of the single bone fractures (either radius or ulna) are associated with a another injury at another level but some of them occur in isolation
Introduction
Examples of a single bone forearm fractures associated with a second injury:
Monteggia fracture dislocation: ulnar shaft fracture with radial head dislocation
Galeazzi fracture dislocation: radial shaft fracture with distal radioulnar joint injury
Essex-Lopresti injury: radial head fracture with distal radioulnar joint injury
Here we will explain both forearm bones fractures and the single isolated forearm bone fractures
Mechanism of injury
A fall on the hand produces a spiral or transverse fracture of both bones usually
A direct blow to the forearm causes a transverse fracture of just one bone (mostly the ulna)
Mechanism of injury
In high energy injuries, the fracture might be comminuted or segmental
Additional displacement is achieved by muscle pull produced by the muscles attached to the radius and ulna, e.g. biceps, triceps, brachialis, supinator, pronator teres, and pronator quadratus
Anatomy

The forearm consist of two bones, radius and ulna which articulate with each through two joints, one proximally through the proximal radioulnar joint and one distally through the distal radioulnar joint
The whole forearm is considered a joint capable of rotation (pronation and supination)
Fractures anywhere on the radius and ulna are considered intra articular fractures
LadyofHats, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Anatomy
The radius and ulna also articulate through hinge joints with the humerus proximally and wrist distally
These joints allow for flexion/extension type of movement, in addition the wrist joint allows for radial and ulnar deviation movements
LadyofHats, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Anatomy
Loss of normal shape of radius or ulna during fractures will result in restriction of the normal pronation/ supination movements

So these bones has to reconstructed perfectly, except in Pediatrics population because pediatrics bones tend to remodel well but still there is specific acceptable displacement criteria that has to be followed
Henry Vandyke Carter  (1831–1897), vectorized and reworked by User:jppialasse, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Anatomy

The muscles of the forearm are contained within compartments separated by fascial envelopes in narrow space (forearm) => there is a risk of compartment syndrome when pressure increases in these compartments especially in high energy injuries
Anatomy
Forearm ligaments include:
The annular ligament in the proximal radioulnar joint
The interosseous membrane in the mid forearm
The triangular fibrocartilage complex in distal radioulnar joint
Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Neurovascular anatomy
Anterior and posterior interosseous nerves
Ulnar nerve
Radial nerve
Brachial artery divides into ulnar and radial arteries
All of those are liable to injury during radial/ ulnar shaft fractures
Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
Symptoms
Patient present with pain and deformity of the forearm
Ask if there is pain in the wrist or elbow
Clinical features
Physical examination
Look
Look for Swelling
Deformity might be seen if there is severe displacement
Inspect the lacerations for any evidence of open fracture
Feel
Feel for tenderness in the forearm , elbow and wrist
Neurovascular examination is done to look for nerve/vessel injury
Clinical features
Move
Patient refuse movement due to pain
Examination is repeated multiple times to exclude compartment syndrome
Imaging
Plain radiographs (AP and lateral) are enough for diagnosis
The radiograph should include the elbow and wrist to detect any injuries to the proximal or distal radioulnar joints
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Treatment
Non operative
Operative
Non operative treatment
It is done by closed reduction and immobilization
Commonly done in pediatrics, and gives excellent results because periosteum is strong and guides reduction process
Non operative treatment is rarely done in adult patients because it is difficult and result in unstable reduction, so operative treatment is superior in adults
Non operative treatment
After closed reduction, The fracture is held in above elbow backslab (to prevent rotation) with elbow at 90 degrees and supported with sling

In cases where the radius is fractured proximal to the pronator teres muscle insertion, the forearm is immobilized while supinated, while in cases where the radius is fractured distal to the pronator teres, the forearm is immobilized while being in the neutral position
Non operative treatment

Neurovascular examination and plain radiographs are repeated shortly after reduction; Plain radiographs are repeated again after a week to make sure no further displacement occurred, and the forearm is immobilized for 6-8 weeks
Exercises are started as soon as pain allows, including hand and shoulder exercises
Operative treatment
Indications:
Failure of closed reduction
Unstable reduction
Open fractures
Operative treatment options include:
percutaneous pinning
ORIF with intramedullary nailing
ORIF with plates and screws (most common)
ORIF with K wire fixation
Operative treatment
ORIF is preferred in adults because reduction is difficult and redisplacement is common except if the fragments are in close contact to each other
Deep fascia is left open to prevent compartment syndrome and only the skin is sutured
After the operation, the arm is kept elevated until the swelling subsides and exercises are started as soon as possible
Complications
Early
Nerve injury: Nerve injuries in elbow dislocations are mostly iatrogenic occur during the surgery
Vascular injury: radial or ulnar arteries can be injuried but it is of no problem since the collateral circulation will satisfy requirements
Damage to the forearm muscles leading to bleeding and swelling, this may lead to higher pressures inside the muscle compartments, impaired circulation and compartment syndrome
Complications
Late
Malunion: occur with closed reduction, there might be angulation, rotation or shortening
Delayed union and non union: those are rare
Complications of plate removal: those are common and they include nerve and vessel damage, infection and refracturing
Complications
Late
Synostosis (cross union): the forearm would be fixed and uncapable of rotation anymore
Stiffness (intraarticular fractures)

text: Introduction
Monteggia fracture-dislocation is any fracture of the ulna associated with a radial head dislocation
Monteggia occur more commonly in children and rarely in adults
Diagnosed by forearm X-rays and treated either operatively or non operatively
Mechanism of injury
Monteggia result from a fall on the outstretched hand with twisting force or a force that lead to hyperextension of the elbow joint
It also can occur from direct blow to the forearm and from high energy injuries
Classification
Classified according to Bado classification
Bado classifies Monteggia fractures according to the direction of the radial head dislocation and the direction of the angulation of the ulna fracture into four types, those include:
Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV
Bado classification
Type I
Anterior dislocation of the radial head + angulated ulna fracture with the apex pointing anteriorly (most common type 60%)
Jane Agnes, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Benoudina Samir, CC BY-SA 4.0 httpscreativecommons.orglicensesby-sa4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Bado classification
Type II
Posterior dislocation of the radial head +  angulated ulna fracture with the apex pointing posteriorly (worst prognosis)
Pfeffer55, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Benoudina Samir, CC BY-SA 4.0 httpscreativecommons.orglicensesby-sa4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Bado classification
Type III
Lateral dislocation of the radial head + ulnar fracture
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Benoudina Samir, CC BY-SA 4.0 httpscreativecommons.orglicensesby-sa4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Bado classification
Type IV
dislocation of the radial head in any direction + fractures of both the radius and ulna
Benoudina Samir, CC BY-SA 4.0 httpscreativecommons.orglicensesby-sa4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
Symptoms
Patient present with pain in the forearm and elbow
Clinical features
Physical examination
Look
Look for Swelling
Deformity of the ulna is obvious, but the elbow deformity is masked by swelling
Inspect the lacerations for any evidence of open fracture
Feel
Feel for tenderness (esp. on the lateral side of the forearm)
Neurovascular examination is done to look for nerve/vessel injury (esp. radial nerve)
Clinical features
Move
Patient refuse movement due to pain
Examination is repeated multiple times to exclude compartment syndrome
Imaging
Plain radiographs (AP and lateral) are enough for diagnosis
The radiograph should include the elbow and wrist to detect any injuries to the proximal or distal radioulnar joints
Jane Agnes, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Imaging
Radial head is dislocated and does not point to the capitulum anymore (because normally the radius points to the capitulum in all elbow X ray views)
Ulnar fracture might by incomplete (greenstick) in children and the radial head is not completely ossified so it can be easily missed on X-rays
Jane Agnes, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Associated injuries
radiocapitellar joint is injured in all of Monteggia fractures
Proximal radioulnar joint is injured in all of Monteggia fractures except in trans olecranon fracture dislocation
Other associated injuries include:
Radial head fracture
Coronoid fracture
Emergency management
Grossly displaced fracture should be reduced in the emergency department
Above elbow backslab is applied to support the fracture and prevent forearm rotation
Treatment
Non operative
Operative
Non operative
Non operative treatment is done in children for the incomplete fractures only (greenstick fractures)
reduction is achieved by restoring the ulna to its normal length by traction
Non operative
Then the forearm is immobilized in above elbow cast for 3 weeks and Re examination is done and radiographs are repeated
Exercises are started as soon as possible
Operative
Operative treatment is done when ulnar fracture is a complete fractures
Operative treatment is achieved with closed reduction of the radial head and ORIF and plating of the ulnar fracture

Radial head is reduced by closed reduction, if it remains stable throughout full range of motion of the elbow then no further management needed; but if it re dislocates or it can’t be reduced then it has to be explored and repaired
Complications
Early
Nerve injury: mostly iatrogenic happen during reduction or during surgery, and they are mostly neuropraxias that will recover on their own
Vascular injury
Compartment syndrome
Complications
Late
Malunion: occur when the ulna is not perfectly reduced which lead to the radial head remains dislocated and limits elbow flexion
Non union: treated by plating and bone grafting
Elbow stiffness: occur especially when the radial head dislocation is missed and when the elbow is immobilized for a longer period of time

text: Introduction
Galeazzi fracture is a fracture of the middle to distal radius associated with a subluxation or dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint
Galeazzi fractures are much more common than Monteggia fractures, Galeazzi account for 7% of all forearm fractures in adults
Radius fractures occurring closer to the wrist are associated with greater instability of the DRUJ
Mechanism of injury
Caused by a fall on the outstretched hand with extended wrist and pronated forearm and a rotational force applied to the body
They also could occur from sports injuries and motor vehicle accidents
Clinical features
Symptoms
Patient present with pain in the forearm and wrist
Clinical features
Physical examination
Look
Look for Swelling, contusions and lacerations
Deformity of the radius or wrist might be obvious
Inspect the lacerations for any evidence of open fracture
Feel
Feel for tenderness over the forearm and wrist
Neurovascular examination is done to look for nerve/vessel injury (esp. median and radial nerves), inquire about weakness, numbness, paresthesia and motor examination
Clinical features
Move
Patient refuse movement due to pain
Examination is repeated multiple times to exclude compartment syndrome
Imaging
X-ray radiographs (forearm AP and lateral) should be ordered and they are enough for diagnosis
A transverse or oblique fracture is seen in the radius with angulation or shortening,
DRUJ is disrupted, signs include:
Widening of DRUJ on AP
Dorsal displacement of the ulna on the lateral view
Ulnar styloid fracture
Radial shortening greater than 5 mm
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Note
The distal radioulnar joint could be injured with isolated radial fracture at any level, or in both forearm bones fractures
Emergency management
Pain management
Gross forearm deformity should be reduced in the emergency department under procedural sedation
Above elbow backslab is applied to support the fracture and prevent rotation
Reassessment of neurovascular status is done
Definitive management
Same as Monteggia, it is important to restore the length of the broken bone
In children, closed reduction is often successful, but in adults closed reduction lead to poor outcomes
That is why in adults, reduction is best achieved by ORIF and plating of the radius and the DRUJ is re examined and re imaged to ensure it is reduced
Definitive management
If the DRUJ is reduced and stable on full range of movement, no further management is needed
If the DRUJ is reduced but unstable then the forearm should be immobilized in the position of stability for the DRUJ (usually supination); K wires maybe applied to support the joint
Definitive management

If the DRUJ is irreducible by closed reduction then open reduction is needed to remove soft tissue interposition or fracture fragment preventing reduction; the triangular fibrocartilage complex and dorsal capsule are then carefully repaired, if there is associated ulnar styloid fracture then it has to be repaired by ORIF
After reduction in all cases, above elbow casting in supination is done for 6 weeks , exercises started as soon as possible
Complications
Early
Vascular injury
Nerve injury
Compartment syndrome: especially in high energy injuries
Muscle tendon entrapment: make reduction difficult
Complications
Late
Malunion
Non union
Radioulnar synostosis
Elbow stiffness

text: Fracture healing is a complex process that involves several stages: hematoma formation, inflammation, soft callus formation, hard callus formation and remodeling
Many factors affect fracture healing , including the diet
And here we will talk about the 10 Foods that delay fracture healing
1. Alcohol
Alcohol interferes with fracture healing by inhibiting the proliferation and differentiation of osteoblasts
Osteoblasts are the cells responsible for formation of new bone
Alcohol also increase the production of inflammatory cytokines leading to prolongation of the inflammatory phase of the healing process
Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
2. High Sugar Foods
Fast foods, deserts, sweets …
Foods high in sugar lead to high blood glucose levels which can cause inflammation and oxidative stress
These effects will prolong the inflammatory phase of the fracture healing process
formulatehealth, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
3. Excessive drinking of Caffeinated Beverages
Tea, coffee, soft drinks …
High levels of caffeine promote calcium excretion in urine and impairs calcium absorption in the intestines leading to Delay in fracture healing
Panamitsu, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
4. Foods high in Salt
High amount of salts promote the excretion of calcium through the kidney leading to delay of the fracture healing
Dubravko Sorić SoraZG on Flickr, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

text: Introduction
Distal radius fractures are common fractures that affect the distal radius
They occur when a significant force is applied to the distal radius and this usually result from falls on the outstretched hand
Distal radius fractures treatment include non operative and operative methods
Anatomy
the radial shaft enlarges as it moves distally (opposite to the ulna)
The distal end of the radius has four different sides, its medial side forms a concavity (the ulnar notch) that accommodates the ulnar head
Its lateral side forms a ridge terminating in the radial styloid process which is larger than the ulnar styloid process
DrJanaOfficial, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Anatomy
Posteriorly we have the dorsal tubercle of the radius which lies between the shallow grooves for the passage of the tendons of the forearm muscles
DrJanaOfficial, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Classification
Distal radius fractures are classified according to the fracture type, location, displacement, joint involvement and associated injuries using radiological assessment
Eponyms names were given to the common fracture types of the radius: e.g. Colles’s fracture , Smith’s fracture …

Although there are approximately 15 different classification systems (e.g. Frykman, AO …) but none appear to be clinically useful; so the normal radiological description and eponyms are used more to describe these fractures
Classification
There are multiple factors that increase the severity of the distal radius fractures, those include:
oblique, spiral, and comminuted fractures
Intra articular fractures
Significant displacement
Associated fractures: distal ulnar fracture , ulnar styloid fracture, or scaphoid fractures
Associated dislocation (e.g. DRUJ dislocation)
Associated ligamentous injury: e.g. scapholunate dissociation
Colles’ fracture
Colles’ fracture is an extra articular fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement
Colles’ fracture is one of the most common fractures to affect the human body
It mainly affect elderly patients after falling on the outstretched hand
Lucien Monfils, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Colles’ fracture
Ulnar styloid fracture is present in 50% of all Colles’ fracture cases
Lucien Monfils, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Smith’s fracture
This is an oblique or a transverse extra articular fracture of the distal radius with volar displacement
It is inherently unstable fracture and require surgical treatment
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Barton’s fracture
This is an oblique intra articular fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement (Dorsal Barton’s) or volar displacement (Volar Barton’s)
This is an inherently unstable fracture
It is associated with dislocation or subluxation of the radiocarpal joint
Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Mikael Häggström, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Chauffeur fracture
This is an isolated intra articular radial styloid fracture caused by loading force on the scaphoid against the radius
This results from starting handle of a car kicking back against the chauffeur’s hand ; same mechanism may result in a scaphoid fracture
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Lunate fossa fracture
Fracture of the volar aspect of the lunate fossa
Lunate fossa provides attachment of the extrinsic carpal ligaments, displacement of this fragment may result in subluxation of the entire carpus
Die punch fragments
Intraarticular fragmented fracture with displacement in form of a step or a gap (Die-punch) that occur due to axial loading force
A section of the articular surface impacted below the level of the adjacent cartilage
These fractures may require delicate manipulation and fixation with levers and wires
Clinical features
Symptoms
Patient present tucking their wrist to the chest and supporting it with the other hand and they complain of wrist pain
Clinical features
Physical examination
Look
Look for Swelling, contusions and lacerations
Deformity maybe clear; Colles’ fracture is associated with dinner fork deformity if there is significant displacement.
Inspect the lacerations for any evidence of open fracture
Feel
Feel for tenderness over the forearm, wrist and hand
Neurovascular examination is done to look for nerve/vessel injury, inquire about weakness, numbness, paresthesia and motor examination
Dsprenkels at nl.wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
Move
Patient refuse movement due to pain
Examination is repeated multiple times to exclude compartment syndrome
Imaging
AP and lateral wrist radiographs are usually enough to make the diagnosis
CT scan is indicated in highly comminuted fractures and for preoperative planning
MRI is helpful for occult fractures and for ligamentous injuries
Imaging
When describing a distal radius fracture; comment on:
Type of fracture
Location
Displacement
Joint involvement
Associated fractures
Lucien Monfils, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Treatment
Non operative
Operative
Non operative treatment
Most distal radius fractures are treated non operatively
Minimally displaced or non displaced fractures are immobilized with a cast for 4-6 weeks or a splint and supported with a sling, the wrist will be slightly flexed with ulnar deviation inside the cast
Fractures with significant displacement will require closed reduction through traction and manipulation and then immobilization with a cast is done for 4- 6 weeks
Non operative treatment
Neurovascular examination is done again after the application of the cast to make sure no further injuries occurred during reduction or cast application
X-ray radiographs are ordered again after the application of the cast to make sure the reduction is good
Exercises are started as soon as pain allows
Operative treatment
Operative treatment is done through percutaneous wires or ORIF with plating or intramedullary nails
Indications
Comminuted fractures
Unstable fractures: fracture re displaces after reduction, fracture with volar displacement (all smith’s and volar Barton’s are considered unstable)
Intra articular fractures with > 2mm displacement
Open fractures
Un reducible fractures
Die punch fracture
Complications
Early
Vascular injury

Nerve injury: median nerve can be damaged during the injury or during the operative treatment and if the symptoms are mild this might be resolved with release of the dressing and elevation but if the symptoms are severe then this suggest acute carpal tunnel syndrome which require urgent intervention through dividing the transverse ligament
Redisplacement: that is why X-rays are ordered again after 1 week
Complications
Early
Compartment syndrome: especially in high energy injuries
Extensor pollicis longus tendon rupture

circulatory problems due to fingers venous circulation not draining well leading to finger cyanosis, that is why fingers must be checked regularly and elevation and finger movements is done to prevent that
Complications
Late
Malunion: fracture unite at abnormal anatomical position
Post traumatic carpal tunnel syndrome
Secondary osteoarthritis: especially in patients with intra articular involvement
Complications
Late
CRPS: common after these injuries, swelling and tenderness of finger joints and vasomotor changes such as altered sweating

Carpal injuries include

More serious unstable tears of the joint capsule and interosseous ligaments
Carpal bones fractures: scaphoid (most common), triquetrum …

In This Video
Normal anatomy of the wrist
Normal anatomy: bones

Surface anatomy
Demonstration on my hand
Normal anatomy: ligaments
Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Normal anatomy: ligaments
Normal anatomy: ligaments
Triangular fibrocartilage complex is a load bearing structure between the ulnar head, lunate and triquetrum , it act as a stabilizer of the ulnar side of the wrist
TFCC is composed of:
Triangular fibrocartilage disc
Extensor carpi ulnaris tendon sub sheath
Ulnotriquetral and ulnolunate ligaments
Ulnocarpal collateral ligament
Radioulnar ligament
Elatmani s, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
TFCC tear
TFCC can get injured in forced ulnar deviation in baseball players or when swinging a rachet

Risk factors for TFCC tear is positive ulnar variance (ulna is longer than radius so the articular surface of ulna is more distal than articular surface of radius) and that occur due to prior surgery or prior fracture
Iiibalesiii, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
TFCC tear

Patient present as ulnar sided wrist pain and maybe clicking or point tenderness between the pisiform and the ulnar head, ulnar deviation reproduces symptoms (TFCC compression test), applying a force across the ulna with the wrist in ulnar deviation reproduces symptoms (press test)
Injurymap, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
TFCC tear
Diagnosed by MRI and arthrography
Treatment is either conservative (rest, NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections) or operative
Operative management indicated if conservative treatment failed or if there is DRUJ instability
Normal anatomy: muscles
Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
Symptoms
Patient present with wrist pain and they report some type of injury mechanism like falling on the outstretched hand, or getting hit by some type of object
InjuryMap, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
Physical examination
Look
Look for Swelling, contusions and lacerations
Deformity maybe seen (in dislocation)
Inspect the lacerations for any evidence of open fracture
Feel
Feel for tenderness over the forearm, wrist and hand
Neurovascular examination is done to look for nerve/vessel injury, inquire about weakness, numbness, paresthesia and motor examination
Clinical features
Physical examination
Tenderness should be carefully localized (blunt end of a pencil is useful for testing for point tenderness)
When the scapholunate ligament is injured => tenderness is present just beyond Lister’s tubercle
for lunate dislocation => in the middle of the wrist
for triquetral injuries => beyond the head of the ulna
for hamate fractures => at the base of the hypothenar eminence
for TFCC injuries => over the dorsum of the ulnocarpal joint.
https://www.scientificanimations.com, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
Physical examination
Move
Movements are often limited (more by pain than by stiffness) and they may be accompanied by a palpable or an audible clunk.
If patient have a good range of active movement on their wrist joint then injury is most likely mild
Imaging
X-rays are the first line investigation modality for carpal injuries
Initially, four standard views are obtained:
PA with wrist in ulnar deviation
Lateral
Semi-pronated oblique
Semi-supinated oblique.
An AP view with the ﬁst clenched is added when the space between the scaphoid and lunate is increased on initial x rays (scapholunate injury).
Imaging
If the initial X-rays are ‘normal’, treat the clinical diagnosis and immobilize the wrist. 10–15% of scaphoid fractures are not visible on initial X-rays.

Early MRI is very helpful in detecting capsule, ligaments and tendon injuries and confirms fracture diagnosis but If MRI is not available, repeated X-rays are needed 2 weeks later (bone resorption and movement can make the fracture more apparent). If there is still doubt then x ray repeated after another 2 weeks
Imaging
In the anteroposterior X-ray note the shape of the carpus, whether the individual bones are clearly outlined and whether there are any abnormally large gaps suggesting disruption of the ligaments.

The scaphoid may be fractured; or it may have lost its normal bean shape and look squat and foreshortened, sometimes with an inner circular density (the cortical ring sign) – features of an end-on view when the bone is hyperﬂexed because of damage to the restraining scapholunate ligament. The lunate is normally quadrilateral in shape but, if it is dislocated, it looks triangular.
Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Mohamed Jarraya, Daichi Hayashi, Frank W. Roemer, Michel D. Crema, Luis Diaz, Jane Conlin, Monica D. Marra, Nabil Jomaah, and Ali Guermazi, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Imaging

In the lateral X-ray the axes of the radius, lunate, capitate and third metacarpal are co-linear, and the scaphoid projects at an angle of about 45 degrees to this line. With traumatic instability the linked carpal segments collapse (like the buckled carriages of a derailed train). Two patterns are recognized: dorsal intercalated segment instability (DISI), in which the lunate is torn from the scaphoid and tilted backwards; and volar intercalated segment instability (VISI), in which the lunate is torn from the triquetrum and turns towards the palm; the capitate shows a complementary dorsal tilt. There may be a ﬂake fracture off the back of a carpal bone (usually the triquetrum) that indicates avulsion of the dorsal radiocarpal ligament.
Imaging
Mikael Häggström, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Imaging
MRI can miss TFCC tears and interosseous ligament tears sometimes
Arthrography is used to look for these injuries
Bone scan will exclude injury if negative but it is not specific if positive
Arthroscopy is helpful in detecting scapholunate or lunotriquetral ligament injuries
Management
‘Wrist sprain’ is a diagnosis of exclusion, when a more serious injury has been excluded with certainty, in serious injuries there is limitation to wrist movement.
Even with apparently trivial injuries, ligaments might be torn and patient may develop carpal instability later.
If the x-ray is normal and clinical picture highly suggest an injury, then immobilize the wrist and request further investigations to look for the injury
Management
immobilization is done with below elbow backslab

The aim is to treat as soon as possible if there is an injury, or to avoid an unnecessary period of immobilization and time from work. If these tests are not readily available, the patient should be re-examined repeatedly until the symptoms settle or a ﬁrm diagnosis is made.

text: Scaphoid fractures
Carpal fractures
Scaphoid fractures (75% of all carpal fractures)
Lunate
Triquetrum
Trapezium
Capitate
Hamate
BodyParts3D is made by DBCLS., CC BY-SA 2.1 JP <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.1/jp/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons
Epidemiology
Scaphoid fractures account for 75% of all carpal fractures

Fractures of other carpal bones are all rare; they can be easily overlooked. Careful examination, X-rays inspection, especially after a significant traumatic mechanism, is important. If in still in doubt, CT or MRI are options.
Epidemiology

A scaphoid fracture occur with a significant traumatic mechanisms, which would typically involve a sporting injury or high-energy fall. That is why it is more common in younger and active individuals.
Scaphoid fractures if missed, they can lead to morbidity as the risk of non-union can be high (14-50% if fracture is displaced)
If left untreated, arthritis, deformity and instability may develop within 5 years which leads to disability
Scaphoid fractures MOI
Scaphoid bone lies in the line of loading between the thumb and forearm
So it can fracture in case of axial loading on the wrist in forced flexion or extension and compression; e.g. fall on the outstretched hand
Laboratories Elsevier via Wikimedia commons
Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Scaphoid fractures
Fractures occur on three anatomical locations on the scaphoid:
Distal tubercule
Waist: 65% of all scaphoid fractures
Proximal pole

Scaphoid blood supply arises from the dorsal distal pole via a branch from the radial artery and the superficial palmar arch so proximal pole gets its blood supply by retrograde flow; so it is considered to have a poor blood supply and less likely to heal than distal pole (high risk of avascular necrosis)
Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
Symptoms
Patient present with wrist pain and they report some type of injury mechanism like falling on the outstretched hand, or getting hit by some type of object
InjuryMap, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
Physical examination
Look
In scaphoid fractures, the wrist appearance looks deceptively normal; but if you look closely, you notice fullness in the anatomical snuffbox

An isolated scaphoid fracture will not usually cause any deformity, but deformity may be seen when associated with a dislocation of the carpus: for example, trans-scaphoid peri lunate fracture-dislocation.
Feel
There is tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox and there is pain on axial loading on the thumb, and pain on pushing the scaphoid tubercle backwards (more specific for scaphoid fractures)
JonRichfield, Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
Physical examination
Move
In scaphoid fractures, there is limitation to wrist movements (more by pain than stiffness)
pain on passive ulnar deviation is highly specific to scaphoid fractures, conversely, lack of pain on ulnar deviation is highly indicative of absence of scaphoid fracture
Classification
Scaphoid fractures are classified according to the Herbert-Fischer classification (most commonly used classification)
Herbert classification is a 4 types classification system and it takes into consideration fracture stability and if it was acute/chronic
Herbert classification provides a guide to the management of scaphoid fractures
Herbert Type A and B are for acute scaphoid fractures while Type C and D for Chronic fractures
Herbert classification
Type A: acute stable fractures
Type A1: Tuberosity fracture
Type A2: Undisplaced Waist fracture
Herbert classification
Type B: acute unstable fractures
Type B1: Oblique distal third fracture
Type B2: Displaced waist fracture
Type B3: Proximal third fractures
Type B4: Fracture dislocation
Type B5: Comminuted fracture
Herbert classification
Type C: Chronic
Type C: Delayed union
Herbert classification
Type D: Chronic
Type D1: Fibrous non-union
Type D2: Sclerotic non-union
Imaging
X-rays are the first line investigation modality for scaphoid fractures
Initially, four standard views are obtained:
PA with wrist in ulnar deviation (scaphoid view)
Lateral
Semi-pronated oblique
Semi-supinated oblique.
All must be carefully examined, often recent fracture only shows in the oblique views (other view are normal)
Imaging
Look at the fracture line (transverse, or oblique)
Look at the location of the fracture line (waist, proximal pole or distal pole)
Look for displacement (translation, angulation or shortening)
If fracture line not visible, treat the clinical diagnosis and repeat x rays after 2 weeks (fracture line shows after a period of time due to bone resorption and movement)
15% of scaphoid fractures are not visible on initial x rays
Imaging

MRI: highly sensitive for detecting scaphoid fractures and also very good in detecting soft tissue injuries such as scapholunate ligament injury; it is used initially if the x rays are normal and clinical examination highly suggest a fracture; but often not available in emergency departments

CT: This is also sensitive for detecting a fracture and is a suitable alternative to MRI. However, the risks associated with radiation must be considered and CT will not identify associated potentially significant soft tissue injuries around the carpus, such as a scapholunate ligament disruption.

Mohamed Jarraya, Daichi Hayashi, Frank W. Roemer, Michel D. Crema, Luis Diaz, Jane Conlin, Monica D. Marra, Nabil Jomaah, and Ali Guermazi, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Emergency treatment
Scaphoid Fractures are managed by: reduce-hold-exercise
There is no role for closed reduction in displaced scaphoid fractures

So emergency treatment is all about holding (immobilization) of the fracture in most cases by a below elbow backslab or a wrist splint and patient is reviewed again after a week in the fracture clinic for assessment and to determine definitive treatment
Emergency treatment

If a patient is suspected to have a fracture but the x rays are normal then patient is reviewed in the fracture clinic after 2 weeks to allow bone resorption and x rays is repeated (better fracture observation on x rays)
Definitive Treatment
Herbert type A1: tuberosity fractures
These are treated in a cast for 4-6 weeks
Non union is rare with these fractures => but if happens, it requires excision of a small fragment or grafting of larger fragment
Type A1: Tuberosity fracture
Definitive Treatment
Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures
These are treated either by casting or by percutanous fixation
Casting: 90% of waist fractures heal in a neutral below elbow POP cast (thumb doesn’t have to be included in the cast) for 6-8 weeks
Type A2: Undisplaced Waist fracture
Definitive Treatment
Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures

After that the cast is removed and wrist is examined clinically and radiologically by x rays, if wrist is painless and x rays is normal then treatment is complete; if still in doubt , CT scan is most reliable for confirming union
Definitive Treatment
Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures
If tenderness on examination is present or fracture line still visible on x ray then cast reapplied for further 4 weeks

After 4 weeks, if wrist is painless and x ray is normal then cast is removed and treatment is complete, if tenderness is present or x rays showing signs of delayed healing (bone resporption and cavitation around the fracture) then bone grafting and internal fixation is indicated
Definitive Treatment
Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures
Percutaneous fixation: it is considered in patients who want faster results (e.g. athletes) but impact and heavy load should still be avoided until fracture is fully healed
Percutaneous fixation is done by cannulated screws that are passed through mall incision in front of the scaphoid tubercle
Definitive Treatment
Herbert type B fractures
Those also can be treated by casting but malunion and non union rates are higher
So it is better to reduce the fracture (closed if possible) and fix it with a compression screw => this will improve the union likelihood and reduce time of immobilization
Herbert classification
Type B: acute unstable fractures
Type B1: Oblique distal third fracture
Type B2: Displaced waist fracture
Type B3: Proximal third fractures
Type B4: Fracture dislocation
Type B5: Comminuted fracture
Herbert Type C and D: Delayed union and non union
This is due to either poor blood supply or displacement of these fractures;
in delayed union fracture line becomes more apparent and hard border develops (making it seem like an extra carpal bone);
in non union cavitation appears on sides of the fracture
Type C: Delayed union
Herbert Type C and D: Delayed union and non union

In distal pole and waist fracture non union, distal fragment rotate forward and proximal fragment rotate backwards giving an appearance of a round scaphoid tubercle (ring sign) on the PA view and dorsally tilted proximal pole and lunate on lateral view (DISI)
Non union of proximal pole doesn’t lead to malalignment but it does lead to avascular necrosis
Herbert Type C and D: Delayed union and non union

Sometimes patient is seen for the first time after an old wrist sprain; x ray shows non united fracture with sclerosed edges maybe several years old, In older patients with low demands or those asymptomatic; non union maybe left untreated if patient agrees after discussion
3-4 weeks of casting may suffice to make patient comfortable once again and no further treatment is required
Herbert Type C and D: Delayed union and non union

In the acute stage of a scaphoid fracture, by 3 months it maybe obvious if the fracture will unite or not; surgery should be advised especially in young patients because it would reduce the chance for osteoarthritis
Surgical options include bone grafting and fixation with K wire or screws and this could be done by open or arthroscopic methods
Complications
Nonunion
Avascular necrosis
Osteoarthritis
Complications
Avascular necrosis
The proximal fragment in scaphoid fractures may undergo avascular necrosis especially in small proximal pole fractures which are far from the scaphoid blood supply
Although revascularization and union are theoretically possible but it is unpredictable and may take many years
Complications
Avascular necrosis

small proximal pole fragments can be stabilized by a very small screw and if there is space, a bone graft from distal radius is inserted and healing is more possible if the graft is attached to an arterial pedicle or the fragment is grafted through arthroscope and stabilized with fine k wires
Complications
Avascular necrosis
If this fails, the dead fragment can be excised but the wrist tends to collapse after this procedure and arthritis develops

A better option would be a proximal row carpectomy (to remove the entire proximal row of carpal bones) or a scaphoid excision and four corner fusion (remove scaphoid and fuse the capitate, hamate, triquetrum and lunate)
SNAC (Scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse)
SNAC is an end stage condition due to vascular necrosis and often requires salvage surgery in the form of a proximal row carpectomy or a wrist fusion
Complications
Osteoarthritis
Non union or avascular necrosis may lead to secondary osteoarthritis of the wrist
If the arthritis is localized to the distal pole, excising the radial styloid may help
Complications
Osteoarthritis
As the arthritis progresses, changes appear in the scaphocapitate joint then in the capitate lunate joint; so stages of arthritis:
Stage 1 radioscaphoid arthritis
Stage 2 scaphocapitate arthritis
Stage 3 lunocapitate arthritis
The lunate radius joint is never affected, thus allowing salvage procedures either a proximal row carpectomy or four corner fusion

text: Carpal dislocations, subluxations and instability

The wrist functions as a system of intercalated segments or links, stabilized by the scaphoid (which acts as a bridge between the proximal and distal rows of the carpus) and the ligaments either side of the lunate (the scapholunate ligament and the lunotriquetral ligament).
Fractures and dislocations of the carpal bones, or even simple ligament tears and sprains, may seriously disturb this system so that the links collapse into one of several well-recognized patterns
Peri lunate dislocation

A fall with the hand forced into dorsiﬂexion may tear the tough ligaments that normally bind the carpal bones. The lunate usually remains attached to the radius and the rest of the carpus is displaced backwards (perilunate dislocation).
Lunate dislocation
Usually the hand immediately snaps forwards again but, as it does so, the lunate may be levered out of position to be displaced anteriorly (lunate dislocation).
Trans-scaphoid perilunate dislocation
Sometimes the scaphoid remains attached to the radius and the force of the perilunar dislocation causes it to fracture through the waist (trans-scaphoid perilunate dislocation).
Clinical features

The wrist is painful and swollen and is held immobile. If the carpal tunnel is compressed, there may be paraesthesia or blunting of sensation in the territory of the median nerve and weakness of palmar abduction of the thumb.
X-rays

Most dislocations are perilunate (Figure 26.18). In the AP view the carpus is diminished in height and the bone shadows overlap abnormally. One or more of the carpal bones may be fractured (usually the scaphoid and radial styloid). If the lunate is dislocated, it has a characteristic triangular shape instead of the normal quadrilateral appearance.

In the lateral view it is easy to distinguish a lunate from a perilunate dislocation. The dislocated lunate is tilted forwards and is displaced in front of the radius, while the capitate and metacarpal bones are in line with the radius.
With a perilunate dislocation the lunate is tilted only slightly and is not displaced forwards, and the capitate and metacarpals lie behind the line of the radius (DISI pattern);
if there is an associated scaphoid fracture, the distal fragment may be ﬂexed.
Treatment
CLOSED REDUCTION
The surgeon pulls strongly on the dorsiﬂexed hand; then, while maintaining traction, then slowly ﬂexes the wrist forwards, at the same time squeezing the lunate backwards with their other thumb.
These manoeuvres usually effect reduction; they also prevent conversion of a perilunate to a lunate dislocation.
A plaster splint is applied holding the wrist neutral. Percutaneous K-wires may be needed to hold the reduction.
Treatment
OPEN REDUCTION
Reduction is imperative and, if closed reduction fails, or if a later X-ray shows that the wrist has collapsed into the familiar DISI pattern, open reduction is needed.

The carpus is exposed by an anterior approach which has the advantage of decompressing the carpal tunnel. A dorsal approach may also be used, which has the advantage of allowing repair of the torn scapholunate ligament.
While an assistant pulls on the hand, the lunate is levered into place and kept there by a K-wire, which is inserted through the lunate into the capitate (Figure 26.19).
If the scaphoid and/or radial styloid are fractured, this too can be reduced and ﬁxed with a headless compression screw or K-wires. Where possible, the torn ligaments should be repaired.

At the end of the procedure, the wrist is splinted in a plaster cast, which is retained for 6 weeks. Finger, elbow and shoulder exercises are practiced throughout this period. The K-wires are removed at 6 weeks.
This injury is frequently accompanied by severe compression of the median nerve, which should be released.
SCAPHOLUNATE DISSOCIATION
Clinical features
A fall on the outstretched hand, rather than breaking a bone, may tear the all-important scapholunate ligament.
There is pain and swelling with tenderness over the dorsum just distal to Lister’s tubercle.
Pushing backwards on the scaphoid tubercle is very painful and, if performed while moving the wrist radialwards and ulnarwards, it can elicit a clunk (‘Watson’s test’).
Imaging in scapholunate dissociation
X-rays

These may, in a signiﬁcant unstable tear, show an excessively large gap between the scaphoid and the lunate. The scaphoid may appear foreshortened, with a typical cortical ring sign. In the lateral view, the lunate is tilted dorsally and the scaphoid anteriorly (DISI pattern). In lesser injuries, a clenched-ﬁst view forces the two bones apart and may reveal the injury.

In children the injury is extremely rare but may be misdiagnosed due to the asymmetric ossiﬁcation seen in the scaphoid particularly. If suspected radiographically, a competent clinical examination will usually reassure the clinician.
Treatment of acute injuries

If the patient is seen early (i.e. less than 4 weeks after injury), the scapholunate ligament should be repaired directly with interosseous sutures, and protected by K-wires for 6 weeks and a cast for 8–12 weeks.
If seen 4–24 weeks after the injury, the ligament is unlikely to heal.

In chronic lesions without secondary osteoarthritis, a ligament reconstruction may be attempted but the results are unpredictable. If there are signiﬁcant symptoms (especially if arthritis develops) a proximal row carpectomy, four-corner fusion or radiosapholunate arthrodesis should be considered.
More information is given in Chapter 15.
LUNOTRIQUETRAL DISSOCIATION

This is a relatively rare injury, much less common than the scapholunate tear. A fall on the ulnar side of thehand followed by ulnar carpal pain, weakness of grip and tenderness distal to the head of the ulna should suggest disruption of the lunotriquetral ligaments.
The physical and X-ray signs may be subtle so the injury is often not diagnosed in the early stage.
X-rays sometimes show a gap or step between the triquetrum and the lunate, with a VISI carpal collapse pattern in the lateral view (i.e. the lunate and scaphoid tilted forwards).
Treatment of acute tears

Acute tears should be repaired with interosseous sutures (Figure 26.19d), supported by temporary K-wires for 6 weeks and a cast for 8–12 weeks. In chronic injuries, a ligament substitution (e.g. a slip of extensor carpi ulnaris) or a limited intercarpal fusion may be considered. For more information, see Chapter 15.

text: Advanced airway support
Airway management is not well covered in textbooks
Airway comes first (ABC) in resuscitation, whatever you do with blocked airway is useless if airway is blocked

Airway include from nasal orifices to alveloli is called airway, but we manage the upper airway in resuscitation which is supraglottic , (everything above glottis) also everything in neck and above , not thoracic (extra thoracic)
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Now let’s talk a little bit about anatomy, so we hav ve nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, laryngeal opening, epiglottis , vallecula (groove)
Airway for it to work normal it has to be
Patent: open
Protected: by neurological reflexes like cough reflex and swallow reflex
Maintained: airway stays open if patient position changed or if time passed
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

In case patient GCS is less than 8, (severe depression in consciousness) , this means that other brain functions also severely depressed, one of these functions is pharyngeal muscles tone (certain brain neurons is continuously discharging to keep pharyngeal muscle tone) , if depressed then tongue will prolapse posteriorly and airway get blocked (airway is not maintained)
In case of angioedema to lips and tongue , this also airway  is not maintained because airway might get  blocked in the future when angioedema reaches the pharynx and larynx

Any problem in patency, protection or maintenance , this need management by creating an artificial airway that has all characteristic of normal airway (patent, protected and maintained) , this is called definitive airway
Definitive airway is a tube that connect the external environment with the trachea and has a cuff inflated below vocal cords
Examples of definitive airways
ETT tube: tube inserted nasally or through the mouth and enters the trachea and it has a cuff inflated below the vocal cords
Ett tube is patent (made of relatively hard material resistant to kinking) , protected by the cuff that prevents secretions from entering the trachea and it is maintained by frequent sectioning
Cricothyroidotomy: you open cricothyroid membrane (between thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage) you go in trachea , it also has a cough below vocal cords
Examples of definitive airways
Tracheostomy: in super sternal notch we open into the trachea, also has a cuff
In emergency department, first choice is ETT tube and if failed you can put a cric or a tracheostomy

Cric is more preferred to tracheostomy in emergency settings, because it is faster to make , in tracheostomy you have to dissect through muscles you might hit a bleeder while in cric you go through a thin membrane into the airway
Tracheostomy can be permanent while cric can’t be left for more than 72 hours because of risk cartilage necrosis due to pressure from the tube
Bedside assessment of the airway
Bedside assessment of the airway is doNe  to see if patient need airway management or no

In assessment of the airway: follow the Steps of Look listen and feel , Same steps Applied in the breathing and circulation assessment and they all done at the same time but in this video we will focus on the airway only

In looking : first think you look at is conscioussness and responsiveness, if patient is unresponsive you follow BLS approach but if responsive then follow ATLS ABCs, color of the patient, look at the mouth , neck and chest of the patient

what is relation of conscioussness to keeping the airway patent , brain is responsible of keeping the conscioussness and the brain does have other functons including keeping the muscle tone which keeps the airway open
conscioussness
if patient is in coma or AMS
coma means GCS of 8 or < with closed eyes
one of the important muscles in keeping the airway patent is the pharyngeal muscles

when we lie supine, gravity pulls down the tongue posteriorly but the pharyngeal muscles tone keep the tongue up and prevent tongue prolapse ; now when there is a pathology that causes disturbance in brain function and patient become unconscious other brain function maybe also get affected including the muscle tone leading to loss of tone and posterior tongue prolapse and blocked airway
so if the patient GCS is 8 or below, this patient is assumed to have impairement in the muscle tone and posterior tongue prolapse
also airway relfexes like the cough relfex in impaired in coma
if patient has altered mental status such as agitation to somnolescence (drowsy), this might be caused by hypoxemia which might be caused by airway obstruction so always look for that
so if you see patient is hypoxemic, exclude airway obstruction as a cause first since it is the most deadly one
CO2 retention is also might be caused by airway obstruction rarely, because most common causes for that is breathing problems
color of the patient

in assessment of the airway you also look at the color of the patient if patient is blue, cyanosis, this is due to increase deoxygenated hemoglobin above 5g/dl and it could be due to airway obstruction, average hb is 15, for cyanosis to occur deoxygenated has to be more than 5; this is also termed severe hypoxemia when spo2 is in 60s

in airway assessment you also look at the mouth, look for scretions coming out (drooling), it could be due to airway related problem esepcially in pediatrics , that is because to swallowe secretions, there has to be a period where glottis closes (respiration stops) to allow secretions to cross, but if patient is dyspnic , this is too much so they let it out drooling and focus on breathing , example is in epiglotitis
mouth
when there is oversecretion of secretions such as in organophosphorous poisoning , this also present problem as it also might lead to aspiration and pneumonia

if the patient is unconscious then you also look inside the mouth if there is foreign body or if there is secretions , (secretions inside the mouth indicate swallow relfex is lose and patient need airway management
foreign body such as fractured tooth or blood clot ; all secretions should be suctioned out
in looking you also look at the face, if there is severe fascial trauma this means patient might need airway management
look at the neck
in looking at the neck , you look for expanding mass (hematoma) in trauma this might compress the airway and lead to obstruction

you also look if patient is using accessory muscles such as scalenus or sternocleidomastoid , this means laboured breathing , you also look at the chest if there is recessions , this also indicates laboured breathing ; laboured breathing is mostly due to breathing problem but it could be due to airway problem too
you also look at the chest if it is moving or not ;
in complete airway obstruction , look for seasaw breathing (paradoxical breathing)
look at the pattern of breathing, chest recessions
Listen
there is a lot of similarities of listening in airway and breathing assessment
but here will talk about the sounds related to the airway only
listening is for abnormal upper airway sounds and speech

first abnormal upper airway sound is stridor, it is mainly an inspiratory sound but could be inspiratory-expiratory, trachea has to be blocked by 90 percent or more to produce stridor sounds (severe obstruction) => airway management is necessary

second sound is gurgling sound , this is due to air passing through secretions, and normally secretions has to be swallowed so if you hear gurgling secretions not swallowed and airway has to be managed
listen

we also can hear a mixed sound between snoring (abnormal sound that get made due to loss of the tone muscles leading to redundant upper soft palate leading to blocked airway when patient is supine , so air to pass it has to push it and Flow leading to the snoring sound which is abnormal due to impaired muscle tone of the upper soft palate or pharyngeal muscles) and gurgling this is called noisy breathing and it is mostly heard in stroke units , those definitely need airway management
listen

in listening , you also listen for the speech of the patient, if patient can speak this means that it is unlikely problem in the airway ; if patient can't complete a sentence and tachypnic then this is mostly a breathing problem but could be due to airway

if patient has a muffled sound after trauma to larynx , then this patient has a direct laryngeal trauma and May need management; if patient can complete a sentence this is due to high respiratory rate possibly due to obstructed airway or problem in breathing

hot potato speech might be due to airway problem In peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) which has to be drained , it also might be due to bulbar and pseudobulbar palsy but that is not related to the airway
feel
in assment of the airway , you feel, all the feel is in the larynx
if larynx is clicking When pressed on , this means it is fractured And in that case patient might need airway management because airway might get obstructed

if there is crackling sensation on the neck, same as when you press on wet sphenga, this is due to surgical emphysema , coming from pleura if there is lung injury or from airway so exclude airway injury as a caused to this emphysema , surgical emphysema is not life threatening because it will spread to all bode subcut tissue because there is no septa between subcut tissue ; but you must look for airway injury (leak)
goal of assessment
to identify if the airway is patent , maintained and protected
When need airway management
when airway is not patent or protected or maintained
airway management is with definitive airway (creating artificial airway)
Modalities of airway management
manuevres
adjuncts => first two are called basic airway management
advanced airway: EGD and ETT tube
surgical airway
maneuvres
a lot of patients come to emergency department in coma
in coma a lot of brain function will be lot including the tone of the pharyngeal muscles
also swallow relfex and cough relfex that protect the airway are also lost
so airway might be obstructed or secretions cause aspiration

first maneuvre you can do to manage the airway is head tilt / chin lift => extension of the head lead to posterior oropharynx get further away from the base of the tongue and airway opened ; chin lift will lift the mandible which is attached to tongue (so lifting the tongue) and opening the airway
maneuvres
head tilt chin lift can't be done in trauma patients suspected for c spine injury because this maneuvre manipulate the c spine into injuring the spinal cord and sebsequent

so instead jaw thrust is done in these patients ; to perform jaw thrust, two emergency providers have to be involved, one to perform the jaw thrust , the other one is to stabilize the head and neck area
jaw thrust is done by both hands on the face, heals are on the zygomatic bone and fingers lift the jaw, thumbs open the mouth
cervical spine motion restriction is the maneuvre done to stabilize the head and neck area
hands of emergency provider on both sides fo the head and catching the shoulders

cervical collars are not enough to stabilize the neck in case of c spine injury, stretchers are used to stabilizee the patient with several straps on their entire body and sandbags on either sides of the head
if patient on cervical collar need airway management, then collar is removed and head is stabilized manually and airway management is done the collar is put back again
airway adjuncts
oropharyngeal airway (OPA)
nasopharyngeal airway (NPA)
oPA is put to bypass the tongue (thus preventing tongue prolapse) , it will provide airway patency but not protection so it is a temporary measure
indication of OPA is coma , the only condition is that patient doesn't have gag relfex
placement is by entering it upside down until it touch the hard palate then it is flipped and entered (to bypass the dome of the tongue)
it can also be inserted by depressing the tongue by tongue dpresseor and inserting the piece

if OPA size is less or more than ideal size for the patient , it might lead to airway obstruction instead of opening, too small might push the tongue into closing the airway and too long might go into the esophagus and block the airway

how to choose the ideal size for the OPA , OPA has to be measured upside down from the angle of the mouth into the angle of the mandible and into the earlobe or it can be measured not upside down from the opening of the mouth into the angle of the mandible
NPA
if patient does have gag relfex then OPA is contraindicated
NPA is longer than OPA for same patient
NPA is indicated if OPA is contraindicated, anything introduced nasally is less gag stimulating

contraindicated if there is fracture base of skull , e.g. otorrhea, raccon, battle sign ; cribriform could be broken and NPA can enter the brain and lead to injury ;; second contraindicated is severe midface fracture which is commonly associated with fracture base of the skull
NPA is measured from infront of the nose and should reach the angle of the mandible or tragus of the ear
NPA is used with water soluble lubricant to prevent injury and then introduced into the nose
if both adjuncts are contraindicated then continue to do maneuvres until you do a definitive airway
always remember maneuvres and adjuncts are just a bridge to the definitive airway
in pediatrics maneuvres and adjuncts has to be done to keep airway open because tongue size is big
Airway assessment and management is one of the most critical interventions that emergency physicians perform.
Intubation is not always necessary, however, and rushing into invasive airway management before initial resuscitation can be problematic.
Rapid airway assessment
Perform a rapid clinical airway assessment which includes
noting the patient’s level of responsiveness,
skin color,
respiratory rate, and
depth of respirations.
Obtain oxygen saturation and capnography unless the patient is in impending or actual cardiac arrest.
The goal is to determine if the patient is maintaining and protecting their airway and meeting critical oxygenation and ventilation goals.
Nothing should be placed in the pharynx to assess gag reflex.
Emergent and immediate decisions on airway management may proceed before obtaining blood gases and x-rays.

text: Advanced airway support: Introduction
Airway management
Airway management is not well covered in textbooks
Airway comes first (ABC) in resuscitation, whatever you do in resuscitation is useless if the airway is blocked
LadyofHats, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Anatomy of the airway

Airway starts from nasal orifices and ends in alveoli, but we manage the upper airway in resuscitation which is supraglottic , (everything above glottis) also everything in neck and above , not thoracic (extra thoracic)
Now let’s talk a little bit about anatomy, so we have nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, laryngeal opening, epiglottis , vallecula (groove)
LadyofHats, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Characteristics of the normal airway
Patent: open
Protected: by neurological reflexes like cough reflex and swallow reflex
Maintained: airway stays open if patient position changed or if time passed
Maintained airway
In case patient GCS is less than 8 =severe depression in consciousness, This means that other brain functions also severely depressed

One of these functions is pharyngeal muscles tone (certain brain neurons is continuously discharging to keep pharyngeal muscle tone) , if depressed then tongue will prolapse posteriorly and airway get blocked (airway is not maintained)
Maintained airway
In case of angioedema to lips and tongue , this also means airway  is not maintained because airway might get  blocked in the future when angioedema reaches the pharynx and larynx
Adebayo PB, Alebiosu OC, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
When to manage the airway

Any problem in patency, protection or maintenance , this will require airway management by creating an artificial airway that has all characteristic of normal airway (patent, protected and maintained), this is called definitive airway
Definitive airway is a tube that connect the external environment with the trachea and has a cuff inflated below vocal cords (to prevent secretions from entering the trachea)
Examples of definitive airways
ETT tube: tube inserted nasally or through the mouth and enters the trachea and it has a cuff inflated below the vocal cords

ETT tube is patent (made of relatively hard material resistant to kinking) , protected by the cuff that prevents secretions from entering the trachea and frequent suctioning and it is maintained because it is open regardless of time and position of the patient
bigomar2, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons
BruceBlaus, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Examples of definitive airways
Cricothyroidotomy: you open cricothyroid membrane (between thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage) you go in trachea , it also has a cuff inflated below vocal cords
Olek Remesz (wiki-pl: Orem, commons: Orem), CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Examples of definitive airways
Tracheostomy: in suprasternal notch we open into the trachea, also has a cuff
In emergency department, first choice is ETT tube and if failed you can put a cric or a tracheostomy
National Heart Lung and Blood Institute (NIH), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Examples of definitive airways

Cric is more preferred to tracheostomy in emergency settings, because it is faster to make , in tracheostomy you have to dissect through muscles you might hit a bleeder while in cric you go through a thin membrane into the airway
Tracheostomy can be permanent while cric can’t be left for more than 72 hours because of risk cartilage necrosis due to pressure from the tube
Resources
Dr. Nasrat Al-Attar emergency medicine teaching videos
Tintinalli’s emergency medicine
Wikipedia

path: D:\Youtube\11 Emergency medicine\1 Rescuscitation techniques\1 Advanced airway support\2 Bedside assessment of the airway\bedside assessment of the airway .pptx
