text: Lactulose
Lactulose is a non absorbable synthetic disaccharide made of galactose and fructose

Lactulose can’t be metabolized in the small intestine so it reaches the large intestine unchanged and that is where it get metabolized by the colonic bacteria to monosaccharides and then to fatty acids, hydrogen and methane
Yikrazuul, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Mechanism of action

Monosaccharides in the colon act as an osmolyte that draws water out of the colon wall (osmotic effect) and it also lead to increased gas formation (methane) => more water and gas in the colon lead to laxative effect => reduction in transit time => treatment of constipation (it is classified as osmotic laxative)
By this mechanism, lactulose work to treat constipation and it is FDA approved for this indication
Mechanism of action
Breakdown of lactulose to short chain fatty acids (e.g. lactic acid and acetic acid) lead to Reduction in PH which facilitates conversion of ammonia NH3 into ammonium NH4+ in the large intestine
Ammonium NH4+ would not diffuse to bloodstream as much as ammonia NH3 diffuses due to its charge; also it can’t cross BBB for the same reason
Mechanism of action
The acidic PH also work to destroy urease producing bacteria involved in the production of ammonia => less ammonia produced
Also, lactulose inhibit intestinal glutaminase activity which blocks the conversion of glutamate to glutamine and its metabolism to ammonia
By these 3 mechanisms, lactulose work to lower blood ammonia and treat hepatic encephalopathy and that is also an FDA approved therapeutic use for this medication
Therapeutic uses
FDA approved therapeutic uses
Prevention and treatment of hepatic encephalopathy, lactulose decreases blood ammonia levels by 25% to 50% and this improve patient mental state
Used as a third line in Management of chronic constipation (after lifestyle modifications and increasing fiber intake have failed)
Therapeutic uses
Off label uses
Management of subacute clinical encephalopathy
Because of its ability to reduce intestinal transit time, lactulose can also reduce deoxycholic acid’s hypersaturation => leading to inhibition of cholesterol stone formation
Pharmacokinetics
Lactulose is available as syrup for oral administration and a rectal enema
Lactulose is poorly absorbed from GI tract and it work locally there
Less than 3% of the total dose is absorbed to the blood and excreted through urine
Adverse effects
Since lactulose doesn’t get absorbed into the blood, it produces side effects limited to the GI tract
The most significant side effect is diarrhea which is dose dependent and decreases in severity with dose reduction
Diarrhea may lead to electrolyte disturbances
Adverse effects
It also may lead to increased bowel sounds, increased flatus, and sensation of bloating
Notes
Lactulose is contraindicated in galactosemia patients requiring galactose free diet
Sorbitol is superior in treatment of constipation in elderly patients
Lactulose may lead to electrolyte imbalances due to its osmotic effect, electrolyte might require monitoring especially in elderly and critically ill patients
Notes
Lactulose may induce lithium toxicity in psychiatry patients due to its ability to induce dehydration through its osmotic action leading to poor renal excretion of lithium

text: Blood enters the nephron from the afferent arteriole to the glomerular tuft and then goes out to the efferent arteriole, the water that going to the bowman capsule is called GFR and normal value is about 125 ml/min,
If we multiply 125 to 60 to 24 we would get the total amount of filtrate per day which is about 180 l/d
The filtrate contains water, different organic compounds, ions except for proteins because the glomerular basement membrane won’t allow it to
And 99% of filtrate is reabsorbed again and that’s why our urine volume don’t exceed 1.5 liters per day
Water is reabsorbed passively and it almost always moves with sodium (salt and water)

65% of filtraeted sodium is actively reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule and of course same amount of water is reabsorbed too, proximal convoluted tubule also actively reabsorbs k, ca, mg, amino acids, organic compounds
Also in proximal convoluted tubule there is secretion of compounds like uric acid which reabsorbed again by the proximal convoluted tubule
Tubular fluid moves after the proximal tubule into the descending part of henle
Then into the ascending part where the na is reabsorbed by 25%  by NaKcc2 transporter and also the part where majority of ca and mg is reabsorbed
The ascending part of loop of henle is impermeable to water, so the descending part is going to absorb the 25% of water
Soo loop of henle absorbe 25% of sodium and water
The filtrate moves to the distal convoluted tubule
By the proximal part of distal convoluted tubule 5-7 % of water and sodium are reabsorbed by na cl transporter and the rest of ca is reabsorbed there by the help of parathyroid hormone
By the distal part of distal convoluted tubule 2- 5% of sodium and water are reabsorbed there by the help of aldosterone in expense of potassium and hydrogen
And there rest of water is reabsorbed by ADH in collecting duct
So diuretics are drugs that make kidney lose water but to make it do that, they have to make it lose sodium in the beginning
We have loop diuretics that work on nakcc2 in loop of henle and that lead to lose of na cl k and water and ca and mg and hydrogen ion
Thizides work on nacl transporter in distal convoluted tubule in lead to lose of na and cl and water
Potassium sparing diuretics work on aldosterone to lose na and h2o and conserve hydrogen and potassium

Second degree burns
The second degree burn involve the epidermis and the dermis and it is on two types:
Superficial partial thickness: extends into papillary dermis (superficial layer of dermis)
Deep partial thickness: extends into reticular dermis (deep layer of dermis)
Superficial second degree burn presentation
Extends into papillary dermis but the reticular dermis is spared
Redness of the burned skin because blood vessels still intact in the reticular dermis
Intense pain because nerve fibers are located in the reticular dermis and it is still intact
Superficial second degree burn presentation
Formation of clear blister (pockets of skin containing fluid)
Themidget17, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Superficial second degree burn presentation
Erythematous and blanch to touch
Moist
Spares hair follicles and sweat glands (both are in the reticular layer of the dermis)
Local infection (cellulitis) is common
Superficial second degree burn healing
Heals without scarring/ minimal scarring
Heals within 7- 14 days
Treatment with cooling the burn with running water for 10-20 min and applying antibiotic ointment and dressing
Deep second degree burn presentation
Injury to epidermis and both layers of the dermis (all the dermis involved)
Appears pale because the blood vessels are in the reticular layer and once injured skin would be pale
Don’t blanch to touch
Less painful, remain painful to pinprick (nerve endings are in reticular layer, once injured pain would be much less)
Dr. med. Peter Illing, Kassel, Germany, CC BY-SA 3.0 DE <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/de/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons
Deep second degree burn presentation
Blisters sometimes present
Dry
Hair follicles and sweat glands might be damaged or destroyed
Deep second degree burn healing
Heals within 2-6 weeks
Severe scarring and contractures
May require excision and skin grafting

text: Burn Assessment
User:Westchaser, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Burn & Trauma Research Center, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Burn assessment
Burn is assessed by calculating the total body surface area affected by the partial thickness (second degree) and full thickness (third degree) burns using one of these methods:
Rule of nine
Rule of palms
Lund and Browder chart
Burn assessment
Superficial (first degree) burns are not included in the calculation of TBSA
Cleaning of debris and soot is mandatory to avoid confusing debris with burns
Calculating TBSA affected by burns benefits
Calculating TBSA affected by burns is helpful in:
Understanding the severity of the burn
Determining the amount of fluid needed for resuscitation using Parkland formula
Nutritional support
Pain management
Infection control
Rule of nine
Originally called Wallace rule of nine relative to the British plastic surgeon alexander Wallace who first developed this method

Mainly used as initial assessment tool in pre hospital and emergency department to estimate the TBSA affected by burn, in burn units the Lund Broader chart is used to re calculate the TBSA again because it is more precise
Quick and easy methods that is used for large surface area burns
Rule of nine
Body part
Estimated body surface area
Adults
Children < 10
Left arm
Right arm
Head & neck
Entire back
Chest & abdomen
Genitals
Left leg
Right leg
Jmarchn, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Rule of nine
Example: if patient right arm and right leg both entirely burned with their chest also burned then
Right arm = 9%
Right leg = 18%
Chest only = 9%
TBSA affected by burn is 36%
Rule of nine
Rule of nine is best accurate in underweight to normal BMI adults
The accuracy is less for children and obese patients
Rule of palm
Best used for burns < 10% TBSA
The size of the patient’s palm (including fingers) equals approx. 1% of patient’s TBSA
Estimation is made by visual assessment
More practical in infants and young children because body surface area is small and easily calculated
Rule of palm
It is also used as initial assessment tool for TBSA in pre hospital and emergency department, Lund Browder chart is then used again to re calculate TBSA in burn units once patient reaches there
Lund and Browder chart
Developed by the American surgeons Charles Lund and newton Browder in 1942
Takes into account the age of the patient (unlike the other methods)
In children, decreasing percentage of TBSA for the head and increasing percentage of TBSA for the legs as the child ages
Best method and most accurate

text: The  amount  of  pain  experienced  by  the  patient  is  often
measured by means of a pain numeric rating scale (NRS) or less
frequently  by  marking  a  line  on  a  100-mm  visual  analog  scale
(VAS, which is more commonly used in research), as well as the
verbal rating scale (VRS) with word descriptors ranging from no
pain to excruciating pain. In each case, values indicate the magni-
tude of pain as mild (1–3), moderate (4–6), or severe (7–10). A
similar scale can be used with children (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry,
Consolability [FLACC] or Wong-Baker scales) and with patients
who cannot speak; the Wong-Baker scale depicts five faces rang-
ing from smiling (no pain) to crying (maximum pain). The Brief
Pain  Inventory  is  a  series  of  questions  regarding  the  severity  of
pain. Functional scales include the Oswestry Disability Index or
the World Health Organization Disability Assessment Scale 2.0.
There are specialized scales for patients with specific conditions
including rheumatoid arthritis and dementia. More comprehen-
sive questionnaires such as the McGill Pain Questionnaire address
the multiple facets of pain including both the affective and sensory
experience.

Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
found in hepatocytes cytoplasm, also found in kidneys, heart and muscles (catalyzes transamination reactions)
ALT is elevated more than AST in most types of hepatitis due to cellular damage
Normal ALT < 50 U/L
ALT elevation
Rise of ALT up to 300 IU/ L is not specific to the liver (it can be due to damage of other organs containing this enzyme)
When ALT rises more than 500 IU/L it becomes specific to the liver
In pregnancy ALT elevate during second trimester but to < 100
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)

Found inside the hepatocellular mitochondria and the cytoplasm too, also found in high concentration in heart, muscle, kidney, brain, pancreas and lungs and that make it less specific indicator of liver injury
Alcohol is a mitochondrial toxin, that’s why in alcoholic liver disease and alcoholic hepatitis AST is much more elevated than ALT
Normal AST < 40 IU/L
AST & ALT elevation ranges and interpretation
If AST & ALT both elevated higher than normal limit and up to < 500 then think of
Cirrhosis
Chronic viral hepatitis
Fatty liver disease
Alcoholic hepatitis
If elevated 500- 1000 then think of
Acute viral hepatitis
Autoimmune hepatitis
AST & ALT elevation
If AST & ALT elevated > 1000 then think of
Shocked liver (ischemia)
Acetaminophen toxicity
AST/ALT ratio
AST/ALT ratio increases in liver function  impairment
AST/ALT ratio is around 1.45 in alcoholic liver disease, 2 in alcoholic hepatitis, 0.9 in non alcoholic hepatitis,
AST/ALT ratio is 4.5 in Wilson disease and hyperthyroidism
AST/ALT ratio is around 1.33 in post necrotic liver cirrhosis
AST/ALT ratio is around 1.17 in viral cirrhosis
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)

enzyme in the cells lining the biliary tract of the liver, it is also found in the small intestine, kidney, bones and placenta, it is important in calcification of bones and lipid transposition in small intestine
ALP elevates in cholestasis (significant elevation) and most of other liver conditions (mild elevation)
Serum ALP also increase in pregnancy (placenta secrete the enzyme), thyroid disease and bone disease
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
Normal range 40- 140
Gamma glutamyl (GGT)
Microsomal enzyme found in hepatocytes, cells lining biliary tract, kidney, pancreas and intestine (almost similar to ALP)
No GGT in the bone so it is not elevated in bone disease (beneficial in differentiating the cause of ALP increase)
If GGT and ALP both elevated then hepatobiliary cause of elevated ALP
Gamma glutamyl (GGT)
Also elevated in cholestasis (significant elevation) and other liver conditions (mild elevation)
Also elevated in heavy alcohol consumption
Elevated in other conditions like DM, acute pancreatitis, MI, Guillian barre syndrome, hyperthyroidism …
Bilirubin
Bilirubin is a waste product from heme breakdown (RBC die and give heme => bilirubin)
Unconjugated bilirubin get conjugated by the liver and gets excreted through bile
Bilirubin gets elevated when there is a problem in the liver because it can’t be excreted anymore
Bilirubin
Normal total bilirubin is 0.1- 1 mg/dL
Normal unconjugated bilirubin is 0.2- 0.7 mg/dl
Normal conjugated bilirubin is 0.1- 0.4
Albumin
Protein made by liver, it is the main protein of plasma proteins
Albumin levels decrease in chronic liver disease (e.g. cirrhosis)
Albumin is a measurement of the synthetic function of the liver, glucose and coagulation factors also measure the synthetic function and all of these decrease in chronic liver disease
Liver test abnormal patterns
Hepatocellular pattern due to problems in hepatocytes, examples are hepatitis and alcoholic liver disease
Cholestatic pattern due to problems in the biliary tract, examples are biliary obstruction and primary biliary cirrhosis
Test
Normal range
Hepatocellular pattern
Cholestasis pattern
ALP
AST
Around 80
ALT
Around 100
Follow up testing
Cholestatic pattern on liver function test:
Best initial test: ultrasound to evaluate biliary ducts
Dilated: extrahepatic cause of obstruction (stone, mass)
Normal: intrahepatic cause of obstruction (primary biliary cirrhosis, pregnancy)
Hepatocellular pattern on liver function test:
Followed by blood tests looking for viral hepatitis and autoimmune hepatitis

text: Acute Liver Failure
https://www.myupchar.com/en, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Liver functions
Liver is responsible for
Detoxification
Support metabolism
Immunity
Digestion
Synthesis of protein such as albumin, coagulation factors…
Definition
Acute liver failure should have all of these elements to be considered acute liver failure :
Severe acute liver injury (hepatocyte necrosis)
Duration is less than 26 weeks
Evidence of encephalopathy: DLOC, change in behavior
Impaired Synthetic function of the liver: abnormal coagulation profile (INR ≥ 1.5)
The patient should not have liver cirrhosis or pre existing liver disease
Causes
When patient present with acute liver failure, think of liver diseases that cause a lot of damage in short period of time
Drug induced hepatitis due to paracetamol ingestion (first most common)
Viral hepatitis (second most common)
Shocked liver (ischemia or hypoxia)
Budd Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis)
Veno occlusive disease
Mushroom ingestion
Causes
Wilsons disease
Sepsis
Autoimmune hepatitis
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
HELLP syndrome
Heat stroke
Malignant infiltration
Causes
Slow progressive liver diseases don’t cause acute liver failure, but rather cause chronic liver failure
NAFLD
Hemochromatosis
Primary sclerosing cholangitis
Primary biliary cirrhosis
Alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency
Pathophysiology
Most causes lead to hepatocyte ATP depletion and cellular swelling => cell membrane disruption
Massive hepatocyte necrosis and apoptosis => liver failure
Signs and Symptoms
Fatigue, weakness
Confusion because of hepatic encephalopathy
Jaundice due to hyperbilirubinemia
Hepatomegaly (liver congestion)
Abdominal pain especially right upper quadrant
Signs and Symptoms
Abnormal LFTs
Abnormal coagulation profile, elevated PT/PTT
Thrombocytopenia due to loss of TPO
Medical history
Comprehensive history helps to exclude DDX, ask for:
Timeline of symptoms and progression
Any history of hepatic disease
Drug history looking for acetaminophen toxicity
Family history looking for Wilson disease and thrombotic disorders
Any recent surgeries looking for possible toxic medications used like some anesthetic agents
Examination
Check vitals looking for hypotension (sepsis)
Abdominal palpation looking for pain and tenderness
Special tests looking for ascites
Altered mental status
Fever (infection)
Diagnosis
Requirements to diagnose Acute liver failure
Evidence of liver injury: Elevated AST/ALT
Evidence of hepatic encephalopathy: change in behavior, decreased level of consciousness, coma
INR more or equal to 1.5
Diagnosis
Follow up investigations
Look for hypoglycemia
Look for hyperbilirubinemia
Low PLT
US to look for Budd Chiari syndrome
Diagnosis
Look for acute kidney injury (elevated urea and creatinine)
Electrolyte abnormalities
Abdominal imaging looking for cirrhosis, features of portal hypertension, hepatocellular carcinoma, vascular problems
Histopathology
Done only if the cause didn’t get identified through history, examination, investigations
Trans jugular liver biopsy taken and examined
Management - Definitive management
Admit to ICU
If you already know the cause then treat the cause
If you don’t know the cause then give N acetylcysteine (paracetamol antidote) and then you can look for the cause
Treat the identified cause
Liver transplantation if treatment not succeeded
Management - Supportive management
IV fluid with controlling acid base balance and electrolytes
Monitor for any bleeding (patient have coagulopathy) and treat with blood products
Blood and urine cultures and start empirical antibiotics if patient have fever
Management - Supportive management
Monitor hepatic encephalopathy and protect airway
Provide nutrition
Monitor for hypoglycemia and maintain blood glucose between 160- 200
Complication
Renal failure
Sepsis
Hypoglycemia

Cerebral edema (most common cause of death in ALF) : edema lead to intracranial hypertension, ischemic brain injury and herniation, triggers include hypoxia, hypotension, decreased cerebral perfusion and increased ammonia levels
Complications
Encephalopathy
Coagulopathy

text: Alcoholic Hepatitis
CDC / Dr. Thomas F. Sellers / Emory University, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Polygon data is generated by Database Center for Life Science(DBCLS)[2], CC BY-SA 2.1 JP <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.1/jp/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons
Alcoholic liver disease stages
Alcoholic fatty liver disease: accumulation of fatty acids in the liver in heavy drinkers
Alcoholic hepatitis: inflammation after binge drinking
Liver cirrhosis: recurrent injuries to the liver caused by alcohol end up with fibrosis
Ashley Pomeroy, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Alcoholic hepatitis
It is hepatitis (inflammation of the liver), it is a severe disease that occur after heavy drinking
Patients mostly have a history of at least 10 years of heavy alcohol drinking
Alcoholic hepatitis can range from mild to severe, mortality in untreated cases is 50% in 30 days
The condition comes suddenly and progress rapidly
Pathophysiology
There is direct hepatocyte damage by alcohol and its metabolites like acetaldehyde

Alcohol damages enterocytes and disrupt the tight junctions between them, this increase intestinal permeability and allows bacteria and fungi to enter portal circulation and travel to liver and cause damage to it too
These two mechanisms acutely lead to alcoholic hepatitis and with time lead to liver fibrosis (cirrhosis)
Signs and symptoms
Fever
Fatigue
CDC, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Signs and symptoms
Jaundice (yellowish discoloration of skin and mucous membranes)
CDC / Dr. Thomas F. Sellers / Emory University, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Signs and symptoms
Abdominal pain, especially right upper quadrant with tenderness
CDC, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Signs and symptoms
Ascites: fluid accumulation in the abdominal cavity
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Signs and symptoms
Hepatic encephalopathy: brain dysfunction due to liver disease, present with
DLOC
Asterixis
Change in behavior
FelipeIbazeta, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Diagnosis
History of heavy alcohol intake
For men, consuming 5 or more drinks on any day or 15 or more per week.
For women, consuming 4 or more on any day or 8 or more drinks per week.
Physical examination reveals tachycardia, tachypnea, fever, hepatomegaly and RUQ pain and tenderness, there might be also spider naevi, muscle wasting, gynecomastia..
LFTs: AST/ ALT ratio is more than 1.5
Diagnosis
AST in most cases between is less than 500 U/L  and ALT is normal
Bilirubin > 3 mg/dL
Liver biopsy not required
US is used to exclude differential diagnosis
Treatment
Abstain from alcohol
Glucocorticoids can be used to suppress inflammation for patients with severe disease (elevated PT/PTT or very high bilirubin)
Nutrition supplementation with proteins and calories
N acetylcysteine
Liver transplantation maybe needed
Alcoholic hepatis vs alcoholic steatohepatitis
ASH is diagnosis based on liver histology while AH is a clinical diagnosis
ASH liver biopsy shows steatosis, infiltration of neutrophils (inflammation) and fibrosis
AH is characterized by history of heavy alcohol consumption until at least 4 weeks before onset of symptoms (jaundice, fever hepatomegaly…)

text: Hernia Treatment
https://www.myupchar.com/en, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
U.S. Navy photo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Principles of hernia treatment
Hernia is treated with surgical repair (there is no conservative therapy for hernia)
Reducible abdominal wall hernia doesn’t necessarily require repair, unless the patient request the repair for symptomatic relief, or for cosmetic reasons
Surgeon might request the repair to establish diagnosis if in doubt
Principles of hernia treatment

Irreducible abdominal wall hernia always require repair, because if not repaired then complications are likely to occur (e.g. bowel obstruction, strangulation and infarction), if patient tolerance for surgery or anesthesia is in doubt (due to morbidity) then irreducible hernia surgery is done only if benefits outweigh risks
All cases of femoral hernia should be repaired because of high risk of strangulation associated with this type of hernia
BruceBlaus, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Principles of hernia treatment
Reducible hernia with increasing difficulty in reduction and increasing size are also indications of surgery
Smaller hernias can be more dangerous than larger ones due to higher risk for strangulation
Surgical approach to hernia
All hernias are treated through following these steps
Reduction of the hernia content into the abdominal cavity with debridement and bowel repair if necessary
Excision and closure of a peritoneal sac if present and reducing it back deep to the muscles
If peritoneal sac is left without it being reduced, there is a risk of fluid formation within the sac (seroma)
Surgical approach to hernia
All hernias are treated through following these steps
Closure of the abdominal wall defect is ideal, but it might be impossible if the defect is large, Muscle flap can be used to close large defects

The defect can be closed with sutures alone but this method is associated with high recurrence rates, additional reinforcement of the defect with a non absorbable mesh is better and lowers the recurrence rates
Mesh used in hernia repair
It is a prosthetic material, it can be a net or a flat sheet
It is used to strengthen the abdominal wall defect, so the abdominal organs and fatty tissues can not protrude through the defect again (it lowers hernia recurrence)
Anpol42, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Mesh types
Synthetic mesh
the most commonly used type
Synthesized from polypropylene, polyester or PTFE
Most of them are non absorbable but there is some that are absorbable but rarely used
Biological mesh
Derived from human or animal dermis, bovine pericardium or porcine intestinal mucosa
Quite expensive
Positioning of the mesh
Mesh should be placed on a firm and well vascularized bed with good overlap with the defect
Mesh could be placed
Onlay: just outside the muscle in the subcut space
Inlay: within the muscle (muscle that has the defect in it)
Extraperitoneal sublay: immediately under the muscle
Intraperitoneal sublay: inside peritoneal cavity
Anpol42, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

text: Neonatal Cyanosis
Author: Jules Atkins, RMSupplied by: Brandi Catt, Attribution, via Wikimedia Commons
Cornelia Csuk, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons
Cyanosis Definition & Types
Bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes
It is on two types: peripheral and central
Peripheral cyanosis is bluish discoloration of distal extremities (hands and feet of the neonate) while the rest of the body is normal in color (pink to white)
Cyanosis Definition & Types

Peripheral cyanosis in newborn for the first 2 days is normal and it is called acrocyanosis and it occurs due to immature control of vascular tone in newborns (vessels in extremities stay dilated, which lead to vascular congestion and bluish discoloration)
The second type of cyanosis is the central cyanosis, it is bluish discoloration of the entire body, especially tongue, mucous membranes and trunk
Cyanosis Definition & Types
Central cyanosis is caused by increase the amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the newborn blood

Central cyanosis in newborn is normal for the first 5-10 minutes after birth, if it persist then it requires immediate evaluation because it reflects serious underlying condition that has to be managed fast
Central Cyanosis Pathophysiology
Cyanosis occurs due to increase the amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the blood due to many causes (will be explained a little later)
Cyanosis become evident at ≥ 3 g/dl of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the neonate blood
If you ask at which oxygen saturation this occurs? It is variable
meg and rahul, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Central Cyanosis Pathophysiology
There is no specific oxygen saturation you would see cyanosis at, because cyanosis depends on amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin

E.g. if the infant has hemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dl, their oxygen saturation has to reach to less than 70% to develop clinical cyanosis (30% of 10 g/dl is 3 g/dl which is the concentration of deoxygenated hemoglobin needed for clinical cyanosis to develop), if the infant hemoglobin conc is 20 g/dl, their oxygen saturation has to reach below 85% for them to develop clinical cyanosis (15% of 20g/dl 3 g/dl)
Central Cyanosis Pathophysiology
There is 5 possible scenarios for deoxygenated hemoglobin to increase (thus leading to cyanosis)
Hypoventilation: Asphyxia
V/Q mismatch: PPHN
Diffusion abnormalities: MAS
Oxygen transport: Methemoglobinemia
Heart problems: TGA
Central Cyanosis Differential Diagnosis
Wide differential diagnosis including:
Hypoglycemia
Sepsis: second most common cause
CVS (third most common cause)
Cyanotic congenital heart diseases: TGA, TOF, truncus arteriosus … => should be identified quickly
Heart failure due to sepsis, myocarditis, SVT, heart block…
Central Cyanosis Differential Diagnosis
RS
RDS: surfactant deficiency (first most common cause)
Transient tachypnea of newborn: self limiting
Meconium aspiration: impairs oxygen diffusion
Diaphragmatic hernia
Pneumothorax
Pneumonia
Persistent pulmonary hypertension
Central Cyanosis Differential Diagnosis
Nervous system
Asphyxia
Intracranial hemorrhage
Neuromuscular disease
Maternal sedative drugs
Meningitis
Blood
Blood loss
Polycythemia
Methemoglobinemia
Peripheral Cyanosis Differential Diagnosis
There is specific differential diagnosis for peripheral cyanosis if it persists for more than 24 hours:
Sepsis
Cardiogenic shock
Hypovolemia
Exposure to cold air or water
What do you do if neonate has central cyanosis on examination
Check ABCs and check vitals
If oxygen saturation is less than 95% then administer supplemental oxygen

Assess for signs of respiratory distress: nasal flaring, chest retractions, tachypnea (more than 60 breaths/min), stridor and grunting, if those are seen on the baby then think of differentials related to respiratory system
What do you do if neonate has central cyanosis on examination
If neonate has weak, irregular or absent respirations then think of differential diagnoses related to heart and nervous system

Hyperoxia test differentiate between cardiac and non cardiac causes of cyanosis (100% oxygen is supplied for neonate for 10 minutes, and their oxygen saturation is checked after, if their saturation increases substantially then the cause pulmonary or CNS related, if their saturation still same then cardiac)
What do you do if neonate has central cyanosis on examination
Take full history from mother (pregnancy history, birth history, medical history)
Do complete physical examination of the neonate
Management
After checking ABCs, Neonate may need respiratory support in form of bag mask ventilation or intubation
Send for CBC (check for anemia and lymphocytosis), blood cultures looking for sepsis, blood glucose looking for hypoglycemia
Send for chest x ray looking for pneumothorax, heart failure
ECG and echocardiogram looking for congenital heart diseases
Management
Manage accordingly

text: Airway foreign body
Foreign body aspiration
Airway Foreign Body is when a foreign body (food or objects) enter the airway and either sit in the larynx or beyond in the trachea or bronchi
Airway foreign body is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among children especially older infants and toddlers (60% of all airway foreign body cases)
Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Epidemiology
Males are 1.7 more likely affected than females
In infants younger than 6 months, the cause is usually secondary to feeding by a well meaning sibling
Epidemiology

Most common aspirated FB are food items (70%): ex. Nuts, seeds, bread and meat, hard candy, gum, bones, raw fruits and vegetables; common inorganic objects aspirated (30%): coins, latex balloons, pins, jewelry, magnets, pen caps, and toys
Globular, compressible or round objects such as grapes, meat and bread, grapes, nuts, balloons, marshmallows and candies can block the airway completely, so they are very dangerous
Epidemiology
Unlike inorganic objects, aspirated vegetable commonly causes intense pneumonitis and subsequent pneumonia and suppurative bronchitis.
Pathophysiology

Young children are more at risk to aspirate a FB because they often use their mouths to explore their surroundings and they are generally more likely to be distracted, playing or ambulatory while eating
Young children are more vulnerable to chocking because they have smaller airway diameter than adults
Clinical features
Clinical features are variable depending on the type, duration, and location of the FB
It ranges from asymptomatic to severe respiratory distress
The most serious complication is complete airway obstruction which manifest in the conscious child as sudden respiratory distress followed by inability to speak or cough
Clinical features
FB Aspiration result in symptoms divided into three stages:
Initial event: paroxysms of coughing, choking, gagging and maybe airway obstruction occur immediately after aspiration of FB, sometimes the child expel the FB during this stage
Asymptomatic interval: the FB becomes lodged, reflexes are fatigued, and immediate symptoms subsides. Lack of symptoms in this stage is deceiving and lead to delayed and missed diagnosis
Complications: airway obstruction, erosions, pneumonia and atelectasis develop which will manifest as fever, cough, hemoptysis …
Clinical features
A FB aspiration should be suspected if there is a history of sudden onset of coughing or choking and should be considered in all children with unilateral wheezing.
At presentation, many patients are in the asymptomatic interval
Classifications
Laryngotracheal FB: patient present with stridor and hoarseness with a FB in the laryngotracheal area
Bronchial FB: patient present with unilateral wheezing and decreased breath sounds with a bronchial FB.
Classifications
Wheeze may be present in 30% of laryngotracheal FB aspirations and stridor in up to 10% of bronchial aspirations.
80% of FBs are in the bronchi.
Patients with immediate onset of severe stridor and cardiac arrest usually have laryngotracheal aspirations.
Diagnosis
Bronchoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis and removal of the foreign body

History is the most important factor in determining the need for bronchoscopy, a positive history must never be ignored but a negative history can be misleading because FB aspiration can be missed and confused with more common causes of respiratory diseases because patients may have fever, wheezing, or rales
Diagnosis
Child caregivers should be asked about nuts and seeds because they are the most common airway FBs
Examination of the nose, oral cavity, pharynx and lung sounds in important
Diagnosis
Radiology also important, plain x rays are the first line, inspiratory PA chest is ordered first, expiratory or lateral decubitus films can assist in diagnosis

90% of FBs are radiolucent and not seen on x rays but secondary findings such as air trapping, asymmetric hyperinflation, obstructive emphysema, atelectasis, mediastinal shift and consolidation all important in identifying location of the FB
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Diagnosis
CT scan has no role in Airway foreign body due to radiation risk in pediatric population although it is highly sensitive and specific and able to detect radiolucent object
So if there is high index of suspicion despite negative or inconclusive imaging, bronchoscopy should be done
Upper esophageal FBs
Upper esophageal FBs are usually radiopaque and can impinge on the posterior aspect of the trachea.
Patients may present with stridor, and typically have dysphagia.
Radiographically, flat FBs such as coins are usually oriented in the sagittal plane when located in the trachea and in the coronal plane when in the esophagus.
Samir, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Treatment
If FB aspiration or airway obstruction is clearly present, perform basic life support (BLS) procedures to relieve airway obstruction (back blows and abdominal thrusts)

If BLS maneuvers fail, perform direct laryngoscopy and extraction of the FB with Magill forceps. If the FB cannot be seen, orotracheal intubation with dislodgement of the FB distally may be lifesaving.
Dctrzl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Treatment
If an obstructive laryngotracheal FB cannot be removed or dislodged, an emergent surgical airway may be required.
Definitive treatment of partial airway obstruction usually requires rigid bronchoscopy in the operating room under general anesthesia by an otolaryngologist or pulmonologist
Complications of rigid bronchoscopy include bronchospasm, bleeding and airway edema

text: Retropharyngeal and lateral pharyngeal abscess
Definition

Retropharyngeal abscess is a collection of pus located in the prevertebral space behind the pharynx (retropharyngeal) while the lateral pharyngeal abscess is located in the lateral part of the pharynx
It can lead to life threatening complications such as airway obstruction or sepsis, so it has to be diagnosed and treated carefully
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Etiology
Retropharyngeal and lateral pharyngeal infections are most often polymicrobial.
The usual pathogens include group A streptococcus, staphylococcus aureus , and oropharyngeal anaerobic bacteria
Etiology
There is increase incidence with methicillin-resistant strains of staphylococcus aureus.
Other pathogens can include Hemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella, and Mycobacterium avium.
Pathophysiology

The retropharyngeal and the lateral pharyngeal lymph nodes that drain the mucosal surfaces of the upper airway and esophagus are located in the neck within the retropharyngeal space and the lateral pharyngeal space
Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Pathophysiology
The retropharyngeal space is located between the pharynx and the cervical vertebrae and extending down into the superior mediastinum
The lateral pharyngeal space bounded by the pharynx medially, the carotid sheath posteriorly, and the muscles of the styloid process laterally
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Pathophysiology

The lymph nodes in these deep neck spaces communicate with each other, and upper respiratory tract infection will infect the lymph nodes, infection spread from one node to the others leading to suppurative adenitis and lymph abscess
Infection of the nodes usually occurs as a result of extension from a localized infection of the oropharynx.
A retropharyngeal abscess can also result from penetrating trauma to the oropharynx, dental infection, and vertebral osteomyelitis.
Epidemiology
Retropharyngeal abscess occurs most commonly in children younger than 4 years of age because the retropharyngeal nodes involute after 5 years of age

This means infection in older children and adults is much less common (because there is no lymph nodes to transmit the infection so infection has to come by trauma, dental infection or vertebral osteomyelitis).
Epidemiology
Abscess formation occurs most commonly in winter and early spring.
Males are affected more than females and approximately two-thirds of patients have a history of recent ear, nose, or throat infection.
Clinical features
Patients with retropharyngeal abscess classically present with fever, irritability, drooling, and dysphagia, and may have inspiratory stridor.
Patients may hold their neck in an unusual position with torticollis, hyperextension, stiffness or the may refuse to move their neck.
Clinical features
The verbal child might complain of sore throat and neck pain.
Other signs can include muffled voice, respiratory distress, or even obstructive sleep apnea.
Clinical features
Physical examination can reveal bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall, and this is present in <50% of infants with retropharyngeal abscess.
Cervical lymphadenopathy may also be present.
Clinical features
Lateral pharyngeal abscess commonly presents as fever, dysphagia, and a prominent bulge of the lateral pharyngeal wall, sometimes with medial displacement of the tonsil.
Diagnosis
Physical examination of the pharynx may show a retropharyngeal mass.
Although palpation commonly will demonstrate fluctuance, this could lead to rupture of the abscess.
Diagnosis
Lateral neck radiograph performed during inspiration with the neck extended may show increased width or an air–fluid level in the retropharyngeal space.
The diagnosis is suggested when the retropharyngeal space at C2-C3 is more than 1/3 vertebral body width or at C4 downward is more than the full width of the vertebral body
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Diagnosis
Deep neck infections can be accurately identified and localized with CT scans, but CT accurately identifies abscess formation in only 63% of patients.
CT with contrast medium enhancement can reveal central lucency, ring enhancement, or scalloping of the walls of a lymph node and help differentiate abscess from cellulitis.
Syed SS, Aderinboye O, Hanson KE, Spitzer ED, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Diagnosis
Scalloping of the abscess wall is thought to be a late finding and predicts abscess formation.
Incision and drainage and culture of an abscessed node provides the definitive diagnosis
Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis includes acute epiglottitis and foreign body aspiration.
In the young child with limited neck mobility, meningitis must also be considered.
Other possibilities include lymphoma, hematoma, and vertebral osteomyelitis.
Treatment
Immediate airway stabilization is the first priority, Intubate unstable patients before performing CT.
Treatment include intravenous antibiotics with or without surgical drainage.
Treatment

Antibiotic choice is controversial because most retropharyngeal abscesses contain mixed flora, A third-generation cephalosporin combined with ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin to provide anaerobic coverage is effective. The increasing prevalence of methicillin-resistant S. aureus can influence empiric antibiotic therapy.

Studies show that >50% of children with retropharyngeal or lateral pharyngeal abscess as identified by CT can be successfully treated without surgical drainage; the older the child, the more likely it is that antimicrobial treatment alone will be successful.
Treatment
Drainage is necessary in the patient with respiratory distress or failure to improve with intravenous antibiotic treatment.
Consider adjunctive treatment with parenteral steroids (e.g., dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg IV to a maximum of 10 mg) to reduce inflammation and edema.
The optimal duration of treatment is unknown, and IV antibiotics are given until the patient has begun to improve, followed by a course of oral antibiotics.
Complications
Complications of retropharyngeal or lateral pharyngeal abscess include significant upper airway obstruction, rupture leading to aspiration pneumonia, and extension to the mediastinum.
Thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein and erosion of the carotid artery sheath can also occur.
Lemierre disease

Another complication is infection of the parapharyngeal space (Lemierre disease), in which infection from the oropharynx extends to cause septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein and embolic abscesses in the lungs.
The causative pathogen is Fusobacterium necrophorum, an anaerobic bacterial constituent of the oropharyngeal flora.
Lemierre disease

The typical presentation is that of a previously healthy adolescent or young adult with a history of recent pharyngitis who becomes acutely ill with fever, hypoxia, tachypnea, and respiratory distress.
Chest radiography demonstrates multiple cavitary nodules, often bilateral and often accompanied by pleural effusion. Blood culture may be positive.
Lemierre disease
Treatment involves prolonged intravenous antibiotic therapy with penicillin or cefoxitin; surgical drainage of extrapulmonary metastatic abscesses may be necessary

text: Peritonsillar abscess
Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is collection of pus behind the tonsil due to infection
It most commonly seen in adolescents and young adults.
It may lead to serious complications such as airway compromise or aspiration pneumronia
James Heilman,MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Etiology
Group A streptococci and mixed oropharyngeal anaerobes are the most common pathogens
More than four bacterial isolates per abscess typically recovered by needle aspiration.
Epidemiology
It is more common than retropharyngeal and lateral pharyngeal abscesses
Pathophysiology
It is caused by bacterial invasion through the capsule of the tonsil, leading to cellulitis and subsequently abscess formation in the surrounding tissues.
Clinical features
The classic presentation is an adolescent with a recent history of acute pharyngotonsillitis who suddenly develops sore throat, fever, trismus, drooling, muffled (hot potato) voice, and dysphagia.
Clinical features
Physical examination reveals an asymmetric tonsillar bulge with displacement of the uvula away from the affected side. As a rule, the affected tonsil is anteriorly and medially displaced.
An asymmetric tonsillar bulge is diagnostic, but it may be poorly visualized because of trismus.
James Heilman,MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Diagnosis
Diagnosis can be made through careful visualization of the oral cavity, there will be uvular deviation away from the abscess, soft palate displacement and localized fluctuance
In toxic appearing patients, examination is not preferred because it may lead to airway compromise and patient referred for CT with contract or ultrasound
But in typical cases, imaging studies are unnecessary
Treatment
Treatment includes surgical drainage, pain control, fluids and antibiotics
Antibiotics should cover group A streptococci and anaerobes. (clindamycin IV or ampicillin/sulbactam IV)
Fluids should be given because patient maybe dehydrated due to decrease oral intake and pain control can be given IV or locally
Treatment
Surgical drainage may be accomplished through needle aspiration, incision and drainage, or tonsillectomy.
Needle aspiration can involve aspiration of the superior, middle, and inferior aspects of the tonsil to locate the abscess.
Intraoral ultrasound can be used to diagnose and guide needle aspiration of a peritonsillar abscess. General anesthesia may be required for the uncooperative patient.
Treatment
Approximately 95% of peritonsillar abscesses resolve after needle aspiration and antibiotic therapy.
The 5% with infections that fail to resolve after needle aspiration require incision and drainage.
Treatment

Tonsillectomy should be considered if there is failure to improve within 24 hr of antibiotic therapy and needle aspiration, history of recurrent peritonsillar abscess or recurrent tonsillitis, or complications from peritonsillar abscess.
A rare complication is rupture of the abscess, with resultant aspiration pneumonitis.

text: Bronchioloitis
Bronchiolitis

Bronchiolitis is inflammation of the small airways (Bronchioles) in infants and very young children < 2 years of age leading to fever, cough, rhinorrhea and wheezing, severe cases develop respiratory distress.
There is no agreed on diagnostic criteria for this illness, and it can be easily misdiagnosed as pneumonia or Asthma
It is mild and self limited in most cases
Annajurlina, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Etiology

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for more than 50% of cases of bronchiolitis. Other agents include human metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, parainfluenza, influenza, bocavirus, and adenovirus.
Viral bronchiolitis is rarely followed by bacterial superinfection.
NIAID, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Risk factors
Preterm infants
Low birth weight
Age < 5 months
Low socioeconomic status
Airway anomalies and chronic lung diseases
Immune deficiency disorders
Parental smoking
Pathophysiology

Infection causes inflammation of the small airways (bronchioles) leading to edema, small airway epithelial cell necrosis and sloughing, increased mucus production and mucus plugs, and bronchospasm, all of these factors increase  resistance in the small airways
Annajurlina, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Pathophysiology

So resistance in the small airways is increased during both inspiration and expiration, but because the radius of an airway is smaller during expiration, this result in wheezing, air trapping, and lung hyperinflation. If the airway is obstructed fully, trapped distal air will be resorbed and the child will develop atelectasis. Hypoxemia is a consequence of ventilation-perfusion mismatch. With severe obstructive disease, hypercapnia can develop.
Epidemiology

Over 100,000 young children are hospitalized annually in the United States with the diagnosis of bronchiolitis, making it the most common diagnosis resulting in hospitalization for children younger than 1 yr.
Epidemiology

Bronchiolitis is more common in males, those exposed to second-hand tobacco smoke, those who have not been breastfed, and those living in crowded conditions. Risk is also higher for infants with mothers who smoked during pregnancy.

Older family members, including older siblings, are a common source of infection; they might experience only minor upper respiratory symptoms (colds) given that bronchiolar edema may be less clinically apparent as airway size increases.
Clinical features
The infant first develops signs of upper respiratory tract infection with sneezing and clear rhinorrhea and may be accompanied by decrease appetite and fever.
Gradually, respiratory distress occur, with paroxysmal cough, dyspnea, and irritability. The infant is often tachypneic, which can interfere with feeding.
respiratory distress manifest as increased Work of breathing, with nasal flaring and subcostal and intercostal retractions, increased respiratory rate
Clinical features
wheezing and crackles usually present and Expiratory time may be prolonged.
Complete obstruction to airflow can eliminate the turbulence that causes wheezing; thus the lack of audible wheezing is not reassuring if the infant shows other signs of respiratory distress.
So Poorly audible breath sounds suggest severe disease with nearly complete bronchiolar obstruction.
Clinical features

Apneic event may precede lower respiratory signs early in the disease, particularly with very young infants. Term infants at a postconceptual age of <44 weeks and preterm infants at postconceptual age <48 weeks are at highest risk for apneic events.
Dehydration can also occur due to poor feeding and tachypnea.
Hypoxemia, cyanosis, altered mental status, are signs of severe disease
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is clinical and does not require laboratory or radiologic studies:
Patients with bronchiolitis are <2 years old (peaking presentation is 6 to12 months of age)
Have an URI (cough and rhinorrhea), and wheezing
Do not have a past history or family history of wheezing or atopic disease
present during an RSV or other respiratory viral pathogen outbreak.
Diagnosis
Chest x rays may show areas of atelectasis in bronchiolitis and may be difficult to distinguish from bacterial pneumonia; so it is quite confusing
And as a result, obtaining chest radiography in a patient whose clinical course and exam are consistent with bronchiolitis may encourage unnecessary antibiotic use.
Matteo Di Nardo, Daniela, Francesca Stoppa, Corrado Cecchetti, Marco Marano and NicolPerrottaa Pirozzi, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Diagnosis
Laboratory testing is also not routinely indicated; the white blood cell and differential counts are usually normal and are not predictive of bacterial superinfection.

Viral testing (polymerase chain reaction, or rapid immunofluorescence) is not routinely recommended in the diagnosis of bronchiolitis but may be helpful if such testing prevents more invasive evaluations.
Diagnosis
Concurrent serious bacterial infection (sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis) is unlikely and confirmation of viral bronchiolitis may prevent the need for a sepsis evaluation in the young febrile infant.

For young children with wheezing in whom the presentation does not clinically fit with the diagnosis of bronchiolitis, including those without other signs of viral infection, with very severe presentation, or complicated clinical course, further workup should be considered (radiology and laboratory tests)
Diagnosis

Children with recurrent or refractory episodes of wheezing in infancy, particularly if associated with failure to thrive, may require evaluation for chronic disorders such as cystic fibrosis or immunodeficiency.
Otitis media is a common complication to bronchiolitis
Differential diagnosis
Asthma: Bronchiolitis and asthma both have wheezing as its most prominent clinical sign.
Most infants with bronchiolitis are unresponsive to both β-agonists and corticosteroids.
Pneumonia: pneumonia can have all the bronchiolitis symptoms but it comes with laboratory findings such as leukocytosis
Treatment
The treatment of children with viral bronchiolitis is supportive management.
Those who are experiencing respiratory distress (hypoxia, inability to feed, apnea, extreme tachypnea) should be hospitalized.
Risk factors for severe disease include younger age, preterm birth, or underlying comorbidity such as cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurologic, or immunologic disease.
Treatment

Hypoxemic children (< 90%)should receive supplemental oxygen. Oxygen can be administered via nasal cannula or Hi-flow nasal cannula in moderate to severe cases or via positive pressure ventilation (CPAP) in severe cases.

Hydration should also be given to children with severe disease. Fluids can be administered intravenously or enterally via nasogastric tube, NG feeding preferred and it is indicated when respiratory rate > 60 breath/min to prevent aspiration
Treatment

Frequent suctioning of nasal and oral secretions often provides relief of distress and improves work of breathing and ability to feed, although this should be limited to the nares or oropharynx because deep tracheal suctioning does not provide additional benefit.
Chest physiotherapy provides no benefit to children with bronchiolitis.
Treatment
Albuterol and corticosteroids are proven ineffective in bronchiolitis; and neither are currently recommended for management.
Nebulized hypertonic saline decreases mucus production and is still used in bronchiolitis although most studies fail to demonstrate it being beneficial
Nasal vasoconstrictors are not indicated and have resulted in tachydysrhythmias.
Treatment

Racemic epinephrine has not been found to improve length of stay or clinical outcomes among inpatients with bronchiolitis, but there is some evidence suggesting it reducing hospitalization rates if used outpatient.

Ribavirin, the only currently available antiviral medication targeting RSV, is also not currently recommended, because of minimal impact on disease outcomes, and because it is costly, difficulty to administer, and associated with multiple toxicities.
Prognosis
Infants with acute bronchiolitis are at highest risk for further respiratory compromise in the first 72 hours after onset of cough and dyspnea.
severity increases over the first 3 to 5 days with total duration of illness 7 to 14 days, So, in severe disease, disposition is done when the patient is well after the 5 day mark
Prognosis

Mortality rate is <1% in developed countries, with death attributable to respiratory arrest and/or failure or severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbances. A majority of deaths due to bronchiolitis occur in children with complex medical conditions or comorbidities such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, or immunodeficiency.
Prevention
Meticulous hand hygiene while dealing with these children is the best measure to prevent transmission of the viruses responsible for bronchiolitis.

Palivizumab, an intramuscular monoclonal antibody to the RSV F protein, may be given as a prophylactic agent. Palivizumab has been demonstrated to reduce risk of hospitalization due to RSV bronchiolitis
Prevention
Palivizumab indications:
In children born at <29 wk completed gestation
In children with significant heart disease or chronic lung disease of prematurity
And it is may be considered in infants with neuromuscular disease and immunocompromised states.

text: Pneumonia in pediatrics
Definition
Causes
Pathophysiology
Clinical features (Signs and Symptoms)
Diagnosis
Treatment
Complications
Pneumonia
Pneumonia, is inflammation of the lower respiratory tract (lung parenchyma)
The etiology, clinical presentation, and severity of pneumonia vary greatly based on the age of the child
Epidemiology
It is the leading infectious cause of death globally among children younger than 5 yr.

Pneumonia mortality is closely linked to poverty, More than 99% of pneumonia deaths are in low- and middle-income countries, with the highest pneumonia mortality rate occurring in poorly developed countries in Africa and South Asia.
Etiology
Infectious
Pneumonia is mostly caused by viruses, RSV and rhinovirus being the most common, others include influenza virus, parainfluenza, adenovirus, metapneumovirus and enteroviruses
In neonates (age 0 to 4 weeks), microorganisms in the birth canal such as group B streptococci, Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, and Listeria monocytogenes are common causes.

S. Pneumonia is the most common bacterial pathogen causing pneumonia in children 4 weeks to 4 years of age while Mycoplasma pneumonia and Chlamydophila pneumonia are most common in children older than 5
S. aureus pneumonia often complicates an illness caused by influenza virus
Etiology
Infectious
In children with HIV (immunocompromised), pneumonia can be caused by M. tuberculosis, salmonella, E. coli, Pneumocystis jiroveci, pseudomonas and cytomegalovirus
Pneumonia caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, which should be considered when the mother had little or no prenatal care.
Pneumonia can also be caused by aspiration (food, gastric acid, foreign bodies, hydrocarbons or lipoid substances), Hypersensitivity reactions and Drug and radiation induced
Pathophysiology

Viral pneumonia usually results from spread of the virus along the airways, accompanied by direct injury to the respiratory epithelium, which results in airway inflammation then obstruction due to swelling, abnormal secretions, and cellular debris.
The small caliber of airways in young infants (can easily get obstructed) makes such patients particularly susceptible to severe infection.
Pathophysiology
Atelectasis, interstitial edema, and hypoxemia from ventilation–perfusion mismatch often accompany airway obstruction.

Viral infection of the lower respiratory tract lead to disturbance of normal host defense mechanisms (which include mucociliary clearance, macrophages and secretory immunoglobulin A) and also lead to disturbance in respiratory microbiota, this ultimately may lead to secondary bacterial infection
Pathophysiology

Bacterial pneumonia most often occurs when respiratory tract organisms colonize the trachea and subsequently gain access to the lungs, and pneumonia can also result from direct invasion of lung tissue due to bacteremia.
When bacterial infection is established in the lung parenchyma, the pathologic process varies according to the invading organism.
Pathophysiology

Mycoplasma pneumoniae attaches to the respiratory epithelium, inhibits ciliary action, and leads to cellular destruction and an inflammatory response in the submucosa. As the infection progresses, sloughed cellular debris, inflammatory cells, and mucus cause airway obstruction, with spread of infection occurring along the bronchial tree, as is seen in viral pneumonia.
S. pneumoniae produces local edema that aids in the proliferation of organisms and their spread into adjacent portions of lung, often resulting in the characteristic focal lobar involvement.
Pathophysiology

Group A streptococcus lower respiratory tract infection typically results in more diffuse lung involvement with interstitial pneumonia. It causes necrosis of tracheobronchial mucosa; formation of large amounts of exudate, edema, and local hemorrhage, with extension into the interalveolar septa; and involvement of lymphatic vessels with frequent pleural involvement.
Pathophysiology

S. aureus pneumonia  manifests as confluent bronchopneumonia, which is often unilateral and characterized by the presence of extensive areas of hemorrhagic necrosis and irregular areas of cavitation of the lung parenchyma, resulting in pneumatoceles, empyema, and, at times, bronchopulmonary fistulas.
Recurrent pneumonia
Recurrent pneumonia is defined as 2 or more episodes in a single year or 3 or more episodes ever, with radiographic clearing between occurrences.
An underlying disorder should be considered if a child experiences recurrent pneumonia
Clinical features

The clinical presentation of pneumonia varies with the age of the patient, although most pediatric patients will have some combination of fever, preceding viral illness, tachypnea, respiratory distress, rales, and diminished breath sounds.
Tachypnea is the most sensitive finding in pediatric patients with pneumonia.
Clinical features

Pneumonia is usually accompanied by respiratory distress which manifest as Increased work of breathing accompanied by intercostal, subcostal, and suprasternal retractions, nasal flaring, and use of accessory muscles is common.
Severe infection may be accompanied by cyanosis and lethargy, especially in infants.
Clinical features
Auscultation of the chest may reveal crackles and wheezing, but it is often difficult to localize the source of these sounds in very young children with hyperresonant chests.
In viral pneumonia, fever is usually present but temperatures are generally lower than in bacterial pneumonia.
It is often not possible to distinguish viral pneumonia clinically from disease caused by Mycoplasma and other bacterial pathogens.
Clinical features
Bacterial pneumonia in older children typically begins suddenly with high fever, cough, and chest pain.
Other symptoms that may be seen include drowsiness with intermittent periods of restlessness, anxiety; and, occasionally, delirium.
In many children, splinting on the affected side to minimize pleuritic pain and improve ventilation is noted; such children may lie on one side with the knees drawn up to the chest.
Clinical features
Abdominal pain is common in lower-lobe pneumonia due to abdominal distention caused by gastric dilation from swallowed air or ileus.
The liver may seem enlarged because of downward displacement of the diaphragm secondary to hyperinflation of the lungs or superimposed congestive heart failure.
Clinical features
In infants, there may be a prodrome of upper respiratory tract infection and poor feeding, leading to the abrupt onset of fever, restlessness, apprehension, and respiratory distress.

These infants typically appear ill, with respiratory distress manifested as grunting; nasal flaring; retractions of the supraclavicular, intercostal, and subcostal areas; tachypnea; tachycardia; air hunger; and often cyanosis.
Clinical features
Auscultation may be misleading, particularly in young infants, with findings disproportionate to the degree of tachypnea.
Some infants with bacterial pneumonia may have associated gastrointestinal disturbances characterized by vomiting, anorexia, diarrhea, and abdominal distention secondary to a paralytic ileus.
Rapid progression of symptoms is characteristic in the most severe cases of bacterial pneumonia.
Diagnosis
For most pneumonias, the etiologic agent is never determined.

The diagnosis of pneumonia should primarily be made on clinical grounds; chest radiography is not required and not considered the gold standard for diagnosis. Chest radiography is not 100% sensitive, nor specific for the diagnosis of pneumonia, and does not distinguish between bacterial or viral etiologies. The presence of fever plus tachypnea, decreased breath sounds, or fine crackles predicts pneumonia with 93% to 96% sensitivity. If all four variables are present, the sensitivity is 98%
Diagnosis
The peripheral white blood cell (WBC) count can be useful in differentiating viral from bacterial pneumonia.
In viral pneumonia, the WBC count can be normal or elevated but is usually not higher than 20,000/mm3 , with a lymphocyte predominance.
Bacterial pneumonia is often associated with an elevated WBC count, in the range of 15,000-40,000/mm3 , and a predominance of polymorphonuclear leukocytes.
Diagnosis
The definitive diagnosis of a viral infection can be done by detection of viral genome or antigen in respiratory tract secretions using PCR assays
The definitive diagnosis of a typical bacterial infection requires isolation of an organism from the blood, pleural fluid, or lung.
Diagnosis
Culture of sputum is of little value in the diagnosis of pneumonia in young children, and percutaneous lung aspiration is invasive and not routinely performed.

Blood culture is positive in only 10% of children with pneumococcal pneumonia and only recommended for children who fail to improve or have clinical deterioration, have complicated pneumonia, or require hospitalization. So they are not recommended for nontoxic-appearing children treated as outpatients.
Diagnosis
Urinary antigen tests should not be used to diagnose pneumonia caused by S. pneumoniae in children because of a high rate of false positives resulting from nasopharyngeal carriage.

Pertussis infection can be diagnosed by PCR or culture of a nasopharyngeal specimen; although culture is considered the gold standard for pertussis diagnosis, it is less sensitive than the available PCR assays
Diagnosis
Ultrasonography is highly sensitive and specific in diagnosing pneumonia in children by determining lung consolidations and air bronchograms or effusions.
However, the reliability of this imaging modality for pneumonia diagnosis is highly user-dependent, which has limited its widespread use.
Diagnosis
Routine laboratory testing is not required for well-appearing children with mild community-acquired pneumonia.
For neonates or older patients with significant respiratory distress or toxic appearance, a blood culture, complete blood count, and serum electrolytes should be obtained.

Rapid viral antigen testing (if available) for RSV, influenza, and human metapneumovirus can be valuable if they are quick and specific, as results may negate the need for imaging, invasive testing, and antibiotic therapy.
Diagnosis

Chest radiography should be reserved for patients in which the differential diagnosis is in question (aspirated foreign body, congestive heart failure, mediastinal mass) or a complication of pneumonia is suspected (failure of outpatient therapy, pleural effusion, cavitary pneumonia, significant patient comorbidities, age <3 months).
Diagnosis
An infiltrate on chest radiograph (posteroanterior and lateral views) supports the diagnosis of pneumonia; images may show a complication such as a pleural effusion or empyema.
Viral pneumonia is usually characterized by hyperinflation with bilateral interstitial infiltrates and peribronchial cuffing.
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Diagnosis
Repeat chest radiographs are not required for proof of cure for patients with uncomplicated pneumonia.
Diawara Zerouali,Elmdaghri,Abid, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Treatment
Treatment of suspected bacterial pneumonia is based on the presumptive cause and the age and clinical appearance of the child.
Neonates and infants younger than 90 days suspected for pneumonia should be hospitalized and given ampicillin + aminoglycoside or third generation cephalosporin (not ceftriaxone)
Treatment

For mildly ill children over 3 months, with mild symptoms, can be treated outpatient with amoxicillin. With the emergence of penicillin-resistant pneumococci, high doses of amoxicillin (90 mg/kg/day orally twice daily) should be prescribed unless local data indicate a low prevalence of resistance. alternatives include cefuroxime and amoxicillin/clavulanate.
Treatment

For school-aged children and adolescents Azithromycin is preferred, while clarithromycin or doxycycline (for children 8 yr or older) are alternatives. For adolescents, a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) may also be considered if there are contraindications to other agents.
Treatment

The empiric treatment of suspected bacterial pneumonia in a hospitalized child requires an approach based on local epidemiology, the immunization status of the child, and the clinical manifestations at the time of presentation.

In areas without substantial high-level penicillin resistance among S. pneumoniae , children who are fully immunized against H. influenzae type b and S. pneumoniae and are not severely ill should receive ampicillin or penicillin G.
Treatment
For children who do not meet these criteria, ceftriaxone or cefotaxime may be used.
If clinical features suggest staphylococcal pneumonia (pneumatoceles, empyema), initial antimicrobial therapy should also include vancomycin or clindamycin.
if infection with M. pneumoniae or C. pneumoniae is suspected, a macrolide antibiotic should be included in the treatment regimen.
Treatment

If viral pneumonia is suspected, it is reasonable to withhold antibiotic therapy, especially for preschool-aged patients who are mildly ill, have clinical evidence suggesting viral infection, and are in no respiratory distress.

However, up to 30% of patients with known viral infection, particularly influenza viruses, may have coexisting bacterial pathogens. Therefore, if the decision is made to withhold antibiotic therapy on the basis of presumptive diagnosis of a viral infection, deterioration in clinical status should signal the possibility of superimposed bacterial infection, and antibiotic therapy should be initiated.
Treatment
Antibiotics should generally be continued until the patient has been afebrile for 72 hr, and the total duration should not be less than 10 days (or 5 days if azithromycin is used).
Shorter courses (5-7 days) may also be effective, particularly for children managed on an outpatient basis.
Studies suggest that a reduction of previously elevated serum procalcitonin levels to an absolute level (0.1-0.25 µg/L) may help determine when to stop treatment.
Treatment
In addition to antibiotics, oral zinc (10 mg/day for < 12 mo, 20 mg/day for ≥ 12 mo given for 7 days) accelerates healing and reduce mortality among children with clinically defined severe pneumonia.
CPAP improves mortality from pneumonia with hypoxemia compared with standard oxygen therapy in settings without access to ventilator derived CPAP or mechanical ventilation.
Treatment
Oxygen should be given for respiratory distress or oxygen saturations less than 90% on room air.
Antipyretics should be administered for febrile patients and may resolve tachypnea associated with fever.
Patients with wheezing should be given bronchodilators.
Treatment
Dehydration (caused by respiratory distress, increased insensible losses, and diminished oral intake associated with pneumonia) should be corrected with boluses of 20mL/kg of normal saline.
Treatment

Neonates with pneumonia have a significant risk for respiratory decompensation and should be admitted and monitored closely, while Most healthy infants (>3 months) and children with pneumonia can be treated as outpatients.

Criteria utilized to determine need for admission include work of breathing (presence of significant tachypnea, retractions, grunting), hypoxemia, poor oral intake, persistent vomiting, dehydration, and social factors (access to follow-up medical care, inadequate family resources, inability to follow treatment plan).
Treatment
Pediatric intensive care consultation and admission should be considered for infants with severe respiratory distress, impending respiratory failure, or shock.
Complications

Complications of pneumonia are usually the result of direct spread of bacterial infection within the thoracic cavity (pleural effusion, empyema, and pericarditis) or bacteremia and hematologic spread.
Meningitis, endocarditis, suppurative arthritis, and osteomyelitis are rare complications of hematologic spread of pneumococcal or H. influenzae type b infection.
Complications
S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, and S. pyogenes are the most common causes of parapneumonic effusions and empyema.
many effusions that complicate bacterial pneumonia are sterile.

Pleural fluid should be sent for Gram stain, and bacterial culture as this may identify the bacterial cause of pneumonia. Analysis of other parameters such as pH, glucose, protein .. (to differentiate exudative from transudative pleural fluid) is not recommended because it doesn’t change management.
Complications
A pleural fluid WBC count with differential may be helpful if there is suspicion for pulmonary tuberculosis or a noninfectious etiology for the pleural effusion, such as malignancy.
Small (<1 cm on lateral decubitus radiograph), free-flowing parapneumonic effusions often do not require drainage but respond to appropriate antibiotic therapy.
Complications

Larger effusions should typically be drained, particularly if the effusion is purulent (empyema) or associated with respiratory distress. Chest ultrasound, or alternatively CT, may be helpful in determining whether loculations are Serous
The mainstays of therapy include antibiotic therapy and drainage by tube thoracostomy with the instillation of fibrinolytic agents (urokinase, streptokinase, tissue plasminogen activator).
Prognosis
Typically, patients with uncomplicated community-acquired bacterial pneumonia show response to therapy, with improvement in clinical symptoms within 48-72 hr of initiation of antibiotics.
Radiographic evidence of improvement lags substantially behind clinical improvement.
Prognosis
when a patient does not improve with appropriate antibiotic therapy, This could be due to:
Complications: such as pleural effusion or empyema
Bacterial resistance
Nonbacterial etiologies such as viruses or fungi and aspiration of foreign bodies or food
Bronchial obstruction from endobronchial lesions, foreign body, or mucous plugs
Preexisting diseases such as immunodeficiencies, ciliary dyskinesia, cystic fibrosis, pulmonary sequestration, or congenital pulmonary airway malformation
Other noninfectious causes including bronchiolitis obliterans, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, eosinophilic pneumonia, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Prognosis
A chest radiograph is the first step in determining the reason for a lack of response to initial treatment.
Bronchoalveolar lavage may be indicated in children with respiratory failure
high-resolution CT scans may better identify complications or an anatomic reason for a poor response to therapy.
Prognosis
Mortality from community-acquired pneumonia in developed countries is rare, and most children with pneumonia do not experience long-term pulmonary sequelae.
Prevention
The introduction of pneumococcal conjugate vaccine resulted in a substantial reduction in the incidence of pneumonia hospitalizations among children.
Influenza vaccine may also prevent pneumonia hospitalizations among children and should be administered to all children >6 mo of age.
Prevention
For infants <6 mo of age, household contacts and other primary caregivers should be immunized.
Maintaining high rates of vaccination for H. influenzae type b, pertussis, and measles remains important for the prevention of pneumonia from these causes.
