text: Meconium Aspiration Syndrome
BruceBlaus, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Definition
MAS is neonatal respiratory distress that occurs when neonate pass meconium in utero leading to meconium stained amniotic fluid and aspirate it during labor resulting in respiratory distress
MAS is diagnosed only if the respiratory distress can not be attributed to another cause like pneumonia, sepsis, TTN, RDS, CHD
MAS symptoms can range from mild RS distress to severe RS distress with respiratory failure
Epidemiology
Meconium stained amniotic fluid is seen in 10-20% of all deliveries
5% of those infants have meconium stained amniotic fluid develop MAS
Mortality is about 2% of MAS infants
MAS is common in infants with breech presentation
Causes
Fetal distress and hypoxia: hypoxic stress on the fetus => enhance intestinal peristalsis and relax anal sphincter => passage of meconium into the amniotic fluid
Fetal maturity: intestinal parasympathetic innervation and myelination increases in later pregnancy => parasympathetic increase intestinal peristalsis => passing of meconium into amniotic fluid
Pathophysiology
Baby passes meconium in utero due to the causes mentioned before
During the delivery process, hypoxia cause the fetus to start breathing and gasping which lead to aspiration of the meconium stained amniotic fluid into the lungs
Pathophysiology

Meconium is thick material (contains cellular debris of skin, GI tract and hair, also contains GI secretions, blood, and mucus) when aspirated, it blocks the respiratory airways (same with foreign bodies), so meconium can cause lung atelectasis when it completely obstruct the right or left bronchi, or it can cause partial obstruction
Meconium triggers inflammation, in 24-48 hours after birth the airways get inflamed in form of chemical pneumonitis and respiratory distress occurs
Pathophysiology
Inflammation lead to inactivation of surfactant => surfactant deficiency lead to increase surface tension of the alveoli => alveoli collapsing => which furtherly aggravate the respiratory distress

Blood supply to the Obstructed airways and collapsed alveoli would be decreased due to vasoconstriction, as an attempt from the lungs to shunt more blood towards the open airways to maintain oxygenation
Pathophysiology

If the previous process occurs extensively in the lungs, this will lead to substantial increase vascular resistance in the lungs which lead to a condition called persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), PPHN may cause right heart failure
All of these factors lead to ventilation- perfusion mismatch => hypoxemia
Pathophysiology
Meconium obstruct airways leading to air trapping, overdistension of the lungs, extra alveolar air leaks and subsequently pneumothorax
Risk factors of MAS
Fetal distress during labor
Post term pregnancy: the greater infant’s gestational age, the greater the risk of passing meconium in utero
Prolonged labor: increase chance of fetal hypoxia
maternal related risk factors: diabetes, hypertension => Placenta problems => increase resistance to blood flow through the placenta => fetal hypoxia
Risk factors of MAS
IUGR
Maternal substance abuse: tobacco, amphetamines or cocaine
Clinical features
A term or post term infant present with respiratory distress and meconium stained amniotic fluid
Respiratory distress present as tachypnea (> 60/m), intercostal and subcostal retraction, nasal flaring, and use of accessory muscles
On physical exam, there might be signs of post maturity like peeling skin, long fingernails and vernix
Diagnosis
Chest x ray shows:
Multiple patchy densities bilaterally
Hyperinflation
Flattening of diaphragm
Atelectasis
Collapsed lung due to pneumothorax
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Cerevisae, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Diagnosis
Oxygen saturation
Arterial blood gas analysis: to evaluate for respiratory failure and acid-base balance
Echocardiography to look for right ventricular dysfunction due to PPHN
Diagnosis
Blood cultures looking for sepsis, empirical antibiotic should be considered
Treatment
Infant born to meconium stained amniotic fluid should have routine postnatal care with monitoring for signs of respiratory distress, endotracheal suctioning is no longer recommended
If infant developed respiratory distress then management is supportive
Oxygen supplementation is needed if oxygen saturation drops below 95%
Treatment
Assisted ventilation techniques are used if the hypoxemia is refractory to oxygen therapy
Blood glucose
Surfactant maybe needed
Nitric oxide is pulmonary vasodilator that can be used in persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Treatment
Glucocorticoids can be used to suppress inflammation
Antibiotics are used if cultures positive
Complications
PPHN
Pneumothorax
Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Prevention
If meconium stained amniotic fluid is seen by obstetrician then obstetrician should suction the infant oropharynx before delivering the rest of their body

text: Neonatal Sepsis
meg and rahul, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Staff Sgt. Matthew Rosine, CC BY 2.5 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5>, via Wikimedia Commons
Definition
Neonatal sepsis is infection involving blood stream with some type of pathogen in newborn infant less than 4 weeks of age.
Neonatal sepsis is a serious illness and it may lead to multi organ failure and death
Neonatal sepsis is classified into
Early onset sepsis (EOS): up to 72 hours after birth
Late onset sepsis (LOS): 72 hours to 28 days
Causes
EOS is caused by transmission of microorganisms from female genitourinary tract to the neonate, this could be:
Either an ascending infection (microorganisms ascend through the birth tract to the uterus and to amniotic fluid and then to baby)
Or neonate could get infected during delivery as they pass through the colonized birth tract
EOS is typically caused by group B streptococci, E. coli, coagulase negative staphylococci, H. influenza, Klebsiella, salmonella and listeria
Causes

LOS is caused by transmission of microorganisms from surrounding environment after delivery, e.g. contact with healthcare workers and caregivers, equipment used early in life like needles, bag masks …
LOS could be a manifestation of an infection transmitted from the mother (vertical transmission)
Causes

LOS is caused by many microorganisms, most commonly by coagulase negative staph (accounts for 50% of LOS cases), could be also caused by bacteria like (H. influenza, S. Pneumonia and Meningococcus) and viruses like (HSV, CMV, enteroviruses)
Pathophysiology

Infants have immature immune system, they have slow inflammatory response, reduced complement activation pathways and show deficit in phagocytic migration to sites of infection, their white blood cells are less effective

Preterm infants also have immature immune system but not just that, they also have deficiency in the amount of immunoglobulins transferred from mother compared to mature infants, this make immature infants at higher risk for sepsis
Pathophysiology
After pathogens infect the blood stream, they might travel to the CNS where they lead to meningitis and encephalitis
5% of neonatal sepsis cases are associated with meningitis
Risk factors for sepsis
Related to the neonate
Preterm infant: weak immune system, immature epithelial barrier, increase need for vascular access => preterm infants are six times more susceptible to sepsis more than term infants
Low birth weight
Poor feeding
Poor cord care
Risk factors for sepsis
Related to the mother
Maternal chorioamnionitis or GBS colonized birth tract
Maternal PPROM
Foul smelling liquor
Maternal fever
Difficult and prolonged labor
EOS signs and symptoms
Initially non specific symptoms
Infant with EOS present in the first 3 days of life with grunting, poor feeding and pallor
Then infant develops lethargy, hypothermia, cyanosis and neutropenia
Respiratory failure, hypotension and meningitis are common in EOS
EOS signs and symptoms
Infant with EOS may also develop DIC, acute tubular necrosis and peripheral gangrene as a complications

Initially it is difficult to differentiate sepsis from RDS because both present with grunting and no lethargy in septic infant initially (a lot of similarities with RDS) => all grunting infants should receive empirical antibiotics until blood cultures arrive
LOS signs and symptoms
Infant with LOS is healthy after birth but then they would comeback after in the period 3- 28 days after birth with non specific symptoms
Then they would develop lethargy and poor feeding
Infants also develop hypotonia, fever, bulging fontanelles and seizures
There is also conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
LOS signs and symptoms
Meningitis occur in 75% of cases

Other complications include osteomyelitis (occur if the cause was group B strep or staph aureus), arthritis (occur if the pathogen was gonococci, staph aureus, candida, many other gram negative bacteria)
When examining LOS infants, focus on examination of bones looking for pseudo paralysis (limitation of movement) of a certain limb
Diagnosis
Septic infants are asymptomatic initially, that is why labs are important for diagnosis
In neonate with risk factors, blood cultures should be drawn
If blood cultures are positive then CSF analysis is indicated looking for meningitis
Diagnosis
CBC, CRP for excluding sepsis
Neutropenia (absolute neutrophils < 1750/ml) is more specific than neutrophilia for sepsis in CBC
Chest x ray to look for pneumonia
If pneumonia is confirmed, ABG is important to monitor for hypoxemia and metabolic acidosis
Diagnosis
Blood pressure and urine output, peripheral pulses and skin color should be monitored to look for septic shock
If septic shock occurs then treatment with fluids and vasopressors
Treatment
Empirical antibiotic therapy should be started if sepsis is suspected (don’t wait for blood cultures to arrive, but at the same time don’t start unless blood cultures are withdrawn)

Typical empirical antibiotic regimens for EOS include IV ampicillin + aminoglycoside (e.g. gentamicin) for 2 weeks, this regimen covers most bacteria in EOS esp. GBS, E.coli and Listeria, alternative option would be ampicillin + cefotaxime
Treatment
For LOS, vancomycin + aminoglycoside should be enough to cover for coagulase negative staphylococci, staph aureus and pseudomonas

If meningitis is expected in EOS or LOS, then most of the previously mentioned antibiotics have poor penetration to CNS, that is why adding a third gen cephalosporin to the regimen is important (e.g. cefotaxime) and treatment period should be extended to 3 weeks
Treatment
Avoid ceftriaxone because it lead to hyperbilirubinemia and cause calcium deposition
If CSF cultures are negative after a while then you can stop the antibiotic treatment at 2 weeks
Treatment
Oral feeding should be withheld, nasogastric tube inserted to relieve distension and aspirate stomach contents
Maintenance fluid therapy and electrolytes replacements are important, parenteral nutrition maybe administered
Assisted ventilation and cardiovascular support maybe needed for the infant to survive
Treatment

If peripheral pulses are weak and capillary refill time is prolonged (normal less than 3 seconds), skin color is pale and urine output is poor then give NS or RL 10 ml/kg over 10 minutes (bolus dose) and repeat 2 times over 45 minutes if needed
If those parameters still poor then dobutamine or dopamine is needed to maintain perfusion
Treatment
Intratracheal surfactant maybe beneficial for the respiratory distress

If the mother birth tract is colonized with group B strep then empirical penicillin prophylaxis is beneficial, also penicillin prophylaxis is beneficial if the mother has other risk factors (fever, preterm labor, previous infant with EOS and chorioamnionitis)

text: Fever and serious bacterial illness
Fever is the most common pediatric chief complaint presenting to an emergency department (ED) and accounts for 30% of outpatient visits.

Infants and children are at relatively high risk for serious bacterial illness (SBI), which includes urinary tract infection (UTI), pneumonia, bacteremia or sepsis, and meningitis—in decreasing prevalence.
Neonates are at the highest risk due to their immature immune response, while infants from 1 to 3 months of age gradually transition to the lower risk profile of older infants and children
Epidemiology
The incidence of UTI is 5% overall in children 2 months to 2 years, with a prevalence of 3% to 8% in all febrile children visiting an ED.

Widespread vaccination has dropped the incidence of occult bacteremia for children 3 to 36 months of age to 0.5% to 0.7%, with further decreases expected with the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine.
Meningitis risk decreases from about 1% in the first month of life to <0.1% later in infancy and childhood.
Clinical features

In the neonate or infant <3 months of age, the threshold for concerning fever is 38°C (100.4°F); in infants and children 3 to 36 months old, the threshold is 39°C (102.2°F). In general, higher temperatures are associated with a higher incidence of SBI.

Immature development may make reliable examination of younger infants difficult. Persistent crying, inability to console, poor feeding, or temperature instability may be the only findings suggestive of an SBI. In the neonate, there may not be any findings other than fever.
Diagnosis and differential Infants <3 months

An ill-appearing infant should be managed aggressively for SBI, with full sepsis evaluation, parenteral antibiotics, and admission, but a well-appearing febrile infant less than 3 months of age presents a challenge because history and physical examination are rarely helpful in diagnosing or excluding SBI in this age group. Meningismus is rarely present; rales may not be appreciated without strong negative inspiratory forces; and bacteremia occurs even in the well-appearing infant. A history of cough, tachypnea, or hypoxemia (by pulse oximetry), however, should alert the examiner to a possible lower respiratory tract infection and consideration of the diagnosis of pneumonia.

All febrile infants 0 to 28 days of age should receive full SBI evaluations, admission, and empiric antibiotic treatment. Antibiotic coverage in this age group includes ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV for Listeria monocytogenes and either gentamicin 2.5 mg/kg IV or cefotaxime 50 mg/kg IV for other common organisms. Avoid using ceftriaxone in this age group. Sepsis testing includes complete blood count (CBC), blood culture, urinalysis and urine culture, and lumbar puncture for CSF indices and culture. Obtain a chest radiograph if any respiratory signs described above are present, and order stool studies if the infant has diarrhea.

Febrile infants 29 to 90 days old without a focal source may be stratified to low or high risk of SBI using one of three classic criteria: Rochester Criteria, Boston Criteria, or Philadelphia Protocol. To meet low-risk SBI status, the infant must be well-appearing with a normal urinalysis and normal White Blood Cell (WBC) count, between 5,000/ mm3 and 15,000/mm3 for the Rochester and Philadelphia, and 5,000/ mm3 and 20,000/mm3 for Boston. A negative CSF (WBC < 10 per hpf in Boston and WBC < 8 per hpf in Philadelphia) is also required for Boston and Philadelphia, and each criteria set has other parameters to complete a low-risk status (Table 66-1). Obtain a chest radiograph for infants with a suggestion of lower respiratory tract disease. Although there is evidence to support the use of any of these three criteria, the overall incidence of bacteremia is dropping due to two factors: empiric antibiotic treatment of women testing positive for Group B streptococcus during the third trimester and the effects from herd immunity from Haemophilus and pneumococcal vaccines.

All ill-appearing infants should receive parenteral antibiotic therapy (Table 66-2) and be admitted to the hospital. Infants older than 28 days at low risk for SBI may be managed conservatively as inpatients with ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM/IV pending cultures; as inpatients without antibiotics; as outpatients with ceftriaxone; or as outpatients without antibiotics. The key deciding factor should be the physician’s comfort level and the ability for close follow-up, typically within 12 to 24 hours. If antibiotics are administered (inpatient or outpatient), obtain CSF and urine and blood cultures prior to administration of antibiotics.

Well-appearing febrile infants between the ages of 29 and 90 days with an identifiable viral source of infection (e.g., respiratory syncytial virus [RSV] or influenza) should have urinary tract infection (UTI) and bacteremia ruled out before being discharged from the ED. Chest radiographs should be obtained at the discretion of the clinician, but are not indicated for well-appearing infants over 29 days with RSV. Consider deferring lumbar puncture if a virus is identified as the cause of the symptoms. Some evidence supports the use of serum biomarkers such as C-reactive protein and procalcitonin to differentiate SBI from viral illness.
infant < 3 months
rochester criteria vs philadelphia protocol vs boston criteria
infants 3 to 36 months

Physical examination findings become more reliable with increasing age, though meningeal signs remain unreliable up to 2 years old. Viral illnesses account for most febrile illnesses in this age group. Diagnostic testing should be guided by clinical findings, including ill appearance; however, UTIs are still prevalent in this age group, even with no focal symptoms besides fever. Females prior to toilet training, circumcised boys younger than 6 months of age, and uncircumcised boys under 1 year of age are at risk for occult UTI. Obtain both a urinalysis and urine culture (by catheterization or suprapubic tap) if a source for the fever is not otherwise identified. Consider CBC and blood culture for bacteremia/sepsis and CSF studies for meningitis, although these are much less common.
Older Febrile Children

The risk for bacteremia in children older than 3 years is <0.2%. CBC and blood cultures are not routinely recommended in immunized older children with fever. Etiologies to consider in older febrile children include viral infections, streptococcal pharyngitis, pneumonia, and sinusitis. Testing is directed by clinical presentation.
emergency Department Care and Disposition

For the management of pneumonia, see Chapter 71; for the management of UTI, see Chapter 75; and infections of the ears, nose, and throat are covered in Chapter 68. Fever is not typically harmful to children, although it makes children uncomfortable and may potentiate seizures. Counsel parents against "fever phobia." To reduce a fever: 1. Remove excessive clothing and blankets to increase heat loss through radiation. 2. Administer acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PO/PR every 4 hours (up to  5 times a day). 3. Consider ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO in children older than 1 year of age; the dose can be repeated every 6 to 8 hours (maximum of 40 mg/kg in 24 hours), and can be given concurrently with acetaminophen.

Patients who are called to return to the ED for evaluation of positive blood cultures require repeat evaluation. Patients with positive blood cultures without contaminants should be hospitalized and treated with parenteral antibiotics. Well-appearing afebrile children already on antibiotics should complete the course of therapy. If the patient is afebrile, clinically well, without a focus of infection, and not currently on antibiotics, repeat testing or treatment is not usually necessary. If the child with a positive blood culture remains febrile or continues to appear ill, a full sepsis workup (CBC, repeat blood culture, lumbar puncture, urinalysis, and urine culture) should be performed. The patient should be hospitalized and given parenteral antibiotics (Table 66-3).

text: Pediatric sepsis
Sepsis (bacteremia with clinical evidence of systemic infection) can rapidly progress to multiorgan failure and death.
Risk factors
Prematurity (immunocompromised state)
Recent invasive procedures
Indwelling foreign objects such as catheters.
Clinical Features
Clinical signs may be vague and subtle in the young infant, including lethargy, poor feeding, irritability, or hypotonia.
Fever is common; however, very young infants may be hypothermic.
Tachypnea and tachycardia are usually present as a result of fever but also may be secondary to hypoxia and metabolic acidosis.
Sepsis can rapidly progress to shock, manifest as prolonged capillary refill, decreased peripheral pulses, altered mental status, and decreased urinary output.
Hypotension is usually a late sign of septic shock in infants and children; sustained tachycardia for age is often the only sign available to the clinician of impending shock.
Diagnosis and Differential
Diagnosis is based on clinical findings and confirmed by positive blood culture results.
Though international criteria for sepsis have been published, all infants who appear toxic should be considered septic.

The laboratory evaluation of a child with presumed sepsis includes CBC, blood culture, complete metabolic panel, blood lactate, catheterized urinalysis with culture and sensitivities, chest radiograph, lumbar puncture, and stool studies in the presence of diarrhea.
Infants are at particular risk for hypoglycemia with SBI and sepsis, and a glucose level should always be checked.
Management

ABCs. Administer high-flow oxygen, institute cardiac monitoring, and secure IV or IO access immediately. Perform endotracheal intubation in the presence of respiratory failure or severe respiratory distress.

Treat shock with 20 mL/kg boluses of 0.9% normal saline solution; preferably 60 mL/kg within 15 minutes. For infants, push actual volumes using multiple saline flushes. Repeat boluses until vital signs, perfusion, mental status, and urine output improve, up to 100 mL/kg total volume.
Treat hypoglycemia with 5 mL/kg 10% dextrose.

4. Initiate antibiotic therapy promptly, as soon as IV access is achieved. Do not delay due to difficulty with procedures such as lumbar puncture. Empiric antibiotic choices include cefotaxime 50 mg/kg IV or piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg IV; because of ceftriaxone-resistant S. pneumoniae, add vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV for ill-appearing infants.
5. Treat volume-refractory shock with dopamine 5 to 20 μg/kg/min or norepinephrine 0.1 to 0.2 μg/kg/min.
6. Consider the presence of drug-resistant organisms, immune-incompetence, or infection with unusual or opportunistic organisms.

text: Croup (laryngotrachobronchitis)
Introduction

Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is the most common infection of the middle respiratory tract (larynx, trachea and bronchi) in children and it is responsible for most cases of stridor after the neonatal period.
Croup is most prevalent in the fall and early winter, and children ages 6 months to 3 years are most affected, with a peak at an age of 12 to 24 months. In adolescents, it manifest as laryngitis
Croup could be mild, moderate or severe but most cases are mild, benign, and self-limited
Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Etiology
The most common causse of croup are parainfluenza viruses (types 1,2,3, and 4) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
Pathophysiology
It lead to inflammation and swelling of the subglottic area which interferes with normal breathing and produces barking cough, stridor and hoarse voice
It affects children because of small trachea diameter which means that a small decrease in this diameter due to inflammation and swelling increase airway resistance and work of breathing
Blausen.com staff (2014). "Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014". via Wikimedia Commons
Pathophysiology
During inspiration, the walls of the subglottic space are drawn together, aggravating the obstruction and producing the stridor
Stridor
Stridor is a harsh, high pitched respiratory sound produced by turbulent air flow through a narrowed trachea
It is usually inspiratory but could be biphasic
It is a sign of upper airway obstruction
Severe croup
Severe croups present with signs of upper airway obstruction
Significant Stridor at rest
Labored breathing
Cyanosis
Marked suprasternal, intercostal and subcostal retractions
Wheezing maybe present if there is associated lower airway involvement
Clinical features

Croup typically begins with a 1-to-3-day prodrome of cough, coryza, inspiratory stridor and low-grade fever, followed by a 3- to 4-day period of classic barking cough, in some cases cough and stridor may be abrupt in onset.
Symptoms peak on days 3 to 4 and are often more severe at night.
Physical examination classically shows stridor, with a greater inspiratory component.
Diagnosis
The diagnosis of croup is clinical: a barking cough, stridor and low grade fever.
Radiographs are not necessary, unless other causes are being considered and Neck or chest radiographs may demonstrate subglottic narrowing or the “steeple sign,”
Frank Gaillard, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Diagnosis
Laboratory studies are not useful in diagnosis, but used to exclude more serious differentials, leukocytosis suggest epiglottis and bacterial tracheitis
Many PCR tests are available for parainfluenza and RSV viruses
Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis includes epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, parapharyngeal abscess
Non infectious differential include foreign body aspiration, laryngomalacia, subglottic stenosis, hemangioma, vascular ring and vocal cord paralysis
Treatment
Patients with significant stridor should be kept in a position of comfort with minimal disturbance; monitor pulse oximetry and provide oxygen as needed.

Dexamethasone reduces symptoms and need for hospitalization in croup and it is administered as one dose orally or IM 0.6- 1 mg/kg (IV formulation can be given orally). Prednisolone can be used as an alternative dosed 2 mg/kg given in two to three divided doses, Nebulized budesonide (2 mg) may also be used.
All patients with croup benefit from corticosteroids Even those with mild symptoms
Treatment

Nebulized racemic epinephrine (2.25%), 0.05 mL/kg/dose up to 0.5 mL, or nebulized L-epinephrine (1:1000), 0.5 mL/kg/dose up to 5 mL, should be used to treat moderate to severe cases (which present with significant stridor at rest).

Epinephrine works by reducing subglottic edema by adrenergic vasoconstriction, temporarily producing marked clinical improvement, peak effect within 10- 30 minutes and fades within 60- 90 minutes and a rebound worsening of symptoms may occur so epinephrine need to be repeated every 20 minutes for no more than 2 hours in severe cases
Epinephrine decreases intubation rates
Treatment
Children with persistent stridor at rest, tachypnea, retractions, or hypoxia, or those who require more than two treatments of epinephrine should be admitted to the hospital.
Complications
Prognosis is excellent and illness last for 5 days
Most common complication is viral pneumonia which occur in 1% of croup cases
Secondary bacterial tracheitis: very rare complication and occur in immunocompromised patients

text: Epiglottitis
Epiglottitis
Epiglottitis (Supraglottitis) is acute inflammation of the epiglottis, and it is a medical emergency because there is a risk of sudden airway obstruction and death
Epiglottis is a piece of tissue located at base of the tongue that prevents food from entering the trachea
藤澤孝志, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
סתו כסלו, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Etiology
Epiglottitis is rare nowadays, because it is mainly caused by Hemophilus influenzae type b, and vaccination (Hib vaccine)  has decreased its occurrence.
Now it is mostly caused Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species and that occur in immunized children. Candida may be a cause in immunocompromised patients.
Clinical features
It is characterized by an acute rapidly progressive course of high fever, sore throat, dyspnea and respiratory distress
The degree of respiratory distress at presentation is variable and lack of respiratory distress at presentation is deceiving and it could be the first manifestation
Hariadhi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
The classic presentation is usually a healthy child suddenly develops sore throat and fever and within hours, the child appear toxic
Swallowing is difficult, breathing is labored and drooling is present
The child may sit in tripod position, sitting upright and leaning forward with chin up and mouth open while bracing on the arms
Hariadhi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Clinical features
A brief period of air hunger and irritability is followed by rapidly increasing cyanosis and coma
Stridor is a late finding and suggest near complete airway obstruction
The barking cough (typical of croup) is rare in Epiglottitis
Usually no other family members are ill with acute respiratory symptoms
Diagnosis
The diagnosis is clinical in patients presenting with the classic presentation
If the diagnosis is uncertain, then lateral neck films should be taken at the bedside in extension and during inspiration with a minimum of disturbance. Thumb sign might be seen
If it is not seen then diagnosis require visualization using laryngoscope in the operating room or in the intensive care unit
Med Chaos, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Diagnosis
The epiglottis is large, cherry red and swollen in epiglottitis

Anxiety provoking interventions such as phlebotomy, IV placement, placing the child supine or direct inspection of the oral cavity should be avoided until the airway is secure because they may lead to airway compromise
If patient require to be transported, a physician skilled in airway management and intubation should accompany the child at all times
Diagnosis
Blood cultures are positive in up to 90% of patients, whereas cultures from the epiglottis are less sensitive.
Treatment

Establish a definitive airway using either endotracheal or nasotracheal intubation or if failed then tracheostomy regardless of the degree of apparent respiratory distress because around 6% of children with epiglottitis without a definitive airway die compared to < 1% of those with a definitive airway

The duration of intubation depends on the clinical course of the patient and duration of epiglottic swelling and extubation is done when swelling subsides, examination is done using direct laryngoscope or flexible fiberoptic laryngoscope
Treatment
intubation usually last for 2-3 days because response to antibiotics is rapid
Treatment
During preparation for intubation by gathering the right personnel and equipment
Keep the patient seated and upright. Provide oxygen and administer nebulized racemic or L-epinephrine.
In the event of total airway loss, attempt bag-valve-mask ventilation.
Treatment
Steroids are used to decrease mucosal edema of the epiglottis. Use methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg IV or dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg IV.

Administer antibiotics: cefuroxime 50 mg/kg/dose IV, cefotaxime  50 mg/kg/dose IV, or ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg/dose IV are appropriate empiric options. In regions with increased cephalosporin resistance, vancomycin 10 mg/kg/dose IV should be added.

text: bacterial tracheitis
Bacterial Tracheitis
Bacterial tracheitis (Aka membranous laryngotracheobronchitis or bacterial croup) is an acute bacterial infection of the trachea that is potentially life threatening
Bacterial tracheitis often follows a viral respiratory infection (especially croup), so it is considered a bacterial complication of a viral disease
By Blausen.com, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Epidemiology
Bacterial tracheitis is uncommon and can present as either a primary or secondary infection.
The mean age of presentation is between 5 and 7 years of age, with slight male predominance.
Bacterial tracheitis is more common than epiglottitis in vaccinated children
Etiology
It is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, S. pyogenes or β-lactamase–producing gram-negative organisms H. influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis.
Anaerobic organisms can also be the cause
Clinical Features

Classic presentation is a child with croup (barking cough, low grade fever and non toxic looking), after a few days of improvement then develops high grade fever and toxicity with respiratory distress (tachypnea, retractions and use of accessary muscles) and stridor, sore throat and cough productive of thick sputum
The patient can lie flat, does not drool and doesn’t have dysphagia (symptoms associated with epiglottitis)
Clinical Features
With this disease there is mucosal swelling at the level of cricoid cartilage, complicated by copious, thick , purulent secretions causing pseudo membranes
Diagnosis and Differential
Diagnosis is clinical: high grade fever, purulent airway secretions and absence of classic findings of epiglottitis
Purulent material is seen below vocal cords during intubation
Blood and purulent material cultures should be taken
Diagnosis and Differential
Lateral neck x rays may show subglottic narrowing of the trachea with irregular densities and ragged and indistinct borders, it may show pseudo membrane detachment in the trachea.
Bronchoscopy used to confirm the diagnosis if still in doubt
Treatment
Nebulized epinephrine (which is very effective in croup) is not effective in bacterial tracheitis
Intubation is required in 50% of patients with this disease, younger patients are more likely to need intubation
Suctioning of purulent materials causes temporary relief but doesn’t sufficiently prevent the need for intubation
Treatment
Provide oxygen

Administer empiric parenteral antibiotics: ampicillin/sulbactam 50 mg/ kg/dose IV or ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg/dose IV plus clindamycin 10 mg/ kg/dose IV. In areas with increasing S. aureus resistance, consider the addition of vancomycin 10 mg/kg/dose IV.
Prognosis
Prognosis is excellent, patient become afebrile within 2 days of empirical antibiotics therapy
Extubation is done when mucosal edema and purulent secretions are decreased

text: PICU - Arrhythmia
Definition
Complications
Treatment
Antiarrhythmic drugs
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus bradycardia
WAP
Extrasystoles
Supraventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia
ecgpedia, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons
Definition
Arrhythmia is disturbance in heart rate or rhythm
Arrhythmia can be congenital or acquired
ecgpedia, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons
Complications
Acute decrease in cardiac output => Heart failure
Degeneration into another arrhythmia such as VF
If continuous may lead to cardiomyopathy
Syncope or sudden death
Treatment
Medications
Transcatheter ablation
Pacemakers
Defibrillators
Antiarrhythmic Drugs
Although majority of antiarrhythmic drugs are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in children; but most are still used off label
Arrhythmia mechanism may be different for the pediatric than the adult population.
Antiarrhythmic Drugs
There may be marked differences in antiarrhythmic drugs pharmacokinetics by age and in comparison, with adults.
Infants may have slower absorption and gastric emptying
Differing sizes of drug tissue compartments affecting the Vd
Hepatic metabolism and renal excretion may vary within the pediatric age-group as well as in comparison to adults
Antiarrhythmic Drugs
Antiarrhythmic drugs are categorized using the Vaughan-Williams classification
This system comprises 4 classes:
Class I includes agents that primarily block the sodium channel, This is further divided by the strength of the sodium channel blockade (a, b, c)
Class II drugs are the β-blockers
Class III includes agents that prolong repolarization by blocking potassium channels
Class IV drugs are the calcium channel blockers
Sertion, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Sinus arrhythmia
Normal physiologic variation in impulse discharges from the sinus node related to respirations
The heart rate slows during expiration and accelerates during inspiration
Occasionally, if the sinus rate becomes slow enough, an escape beat arises from the atrioventricular junction
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia characteristics
Variation in P-P interval
No change in P-wave morphology
No change in PR interval
Rocuronium Bromide, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Sinus bradycardia
Slow discharge of impulses from the sinus node,
Rate <90 in neonates and <60 in older children
Sinus bradycardia
Maybe associated with hypothyroidism, conditions with high vagal tone such as GIT obstruction or elevated intracranial pressure
Frequently associated with junctional escape beats and premature atrial contractions.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia characteristics:
P wave is present (sinus rhythm)
Rate is below 90 for neonates and 60 for infants and children
James Heilman, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Wandering atrial pacemaker
Intermittent shift in the pacemaker of the heart from the sinus node to another part of the atrium.
It may also be seen in association with sinus bradycardia in which the shift in atrial focus is an escape phenomenon.
Wandering atrial pacemaker
Wandering atrial pacemaker characteristics:
P wave is present but it differs in shape between beats (depending on its origin if it is sinus or atrial)
There maybe fusion between the sinus P and the ectopic atrial pacemaker
Rocuronium Bromide, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Extrasystole
Produced by the premature discharge of an ectopic focus that may be situated in the atrium, the AV junction, or the ventricle.
Divided into premature atrial contractions (PACs) and premature ventricular contractions (PVCs)
Isolated extrasystoles are of no clinical or prognostic significance, while frequent extrasystoles may be caused by organic heart disease (inflammation, ischemia, fibrosis) or drug toxicity.
PACs
Common in childhood, in the absence of cardiac disease.
Depending on the degree of prematurity of the beat and preceding R-R interval, PACs may result in a normal, a prolonged (aberrancy), or an absent (blocked PAC) QRS complex.
PACs
ECG shows either a premature P wave superimposed on and deforming the preceding T wave or a P wave that is premature and has a different contour from that of the other sinus P waves.
PACs may reset the sinus node pacemaker, leading to an incomplete compensatory pause
PVCs
Arise in any region of the ventricles.
Characterized by premature, widened, bizarre QRS complexes that are not preceded by a premature P wave.
Classified into uniform and multiform
PVCs
Often, but not always, followed by a full compensatory pause.
Presence of fusion beats proves the ventricular origin of the premature beat.
YitzhakNat, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Extrasystoles
Extrasystoles produce a smaller stroke and pulse volume than normal
Frequent, extrasystoles may lead to a definite rhythm, e.g., Bigeminy and trigeminy
Daniel Nofftz, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Extrasystoles

Most patients are unaware of single PVCs, while some may be aware of a “skipped beat” over the precordium. This sensation is caused by the increased stroke volume of the normal beat +after a compensatory pause.
Anxiety, a febrile illness, or ingestion of various drugs or stimulants may exacerbate PVCs.
It is important to distinguish PVCs that are benign from those that are likely to lead to more severe arrhythmias.
Criteria to furtherly investigate PVCs or not
≥2 PVCs in a row
Multiform PVCs
Increased ventricular ectopic activity with exercise
R-on-T phenomenon
Extreme frequency of beats
Presence of underlying heart disease, a history of heart surgery, or both.
Treatment
Benign PVCs is reassurance
Malignant PVCs are usually secondary to another medical problem
Treat the underlying cause
Lidocaine, amiodarone …
Tachycardias
Supraventricular
Ventricular
Madhero88 CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
AVRT
Occur in presence of an accessory pathway
in conditions such as WPW syndrome
WPW syndrome
AVNRT
SVT Treatment
Vagal stimulation Valsalva maneuver, straining, breath holding, or standing on their head
Adenosine, DC
Refractory SVT
Holter monitoring
EPS studies
Atrial ectopic tachycardia
Tachycardia originating in a single focus in the atria
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Originating from multiple different foci within the atria > 3
Common in infants without cardiac disease
Goal is to slow the ventricular rate
Accelerated junctional ectopic tachycardia (JET)
Automatic (non reentry) arrhythmia in which junctional rate > sinus node rate
Occur in early postoperative period after cardiac surgery
Reduction of infusion rate of catecholamines and control of fever and pain, amiodarone, sotalol
Atrial flutter
Supraventricular tachycardia
Intraatrial reentry circuit at a rate of 250-300 in children, 400-600 in neonates
AV node cannot transmit rapid impulses, so some AV block is always present
Treatment
DC cardioversion
Anticoagulation before conversion
B blockers , CCB
Class I and III antiarrhythmics
Catheter ablation
Atrial fibillation
Supraventricular tachycardia
Intraatrial reentry circuit that is more chaotic at a rate of 400-700 beats/min
Produces an irregularly irregular ventricular response and pulse
Ventricular tachycardia
at least 3 consecutive PVCs at >120 beats/min
paroxysmal or incessant
Associated with cardiac disease, prolonged QT interval, WPW syndrome and drug use
Treatment
DC cardioversion
Amiodarone, lidocaine, procainamide
Temporary or permanent pacemaker
Ventricular fibrillation
Chaotic intra ventricular reentry rhythm that result in cardiac arrest
CPR and DC defibrillation
Amiodarone or lidocaine
Long QT syndromes
QTc interval > 480ms
Long QT is associated with torsades de pointes and VF => syncope and sudden death
Types
Mutations in cardiac potassium and sodium channels
13 variants of long QT syndrome = LQT1, LQT2 …
LQT 1 induced by stress or exertion, LQT3 induced by sleep
Treated by B blockers , pacemaker due to bradycardia
ICD implantation
Short QT syndromes
Atrial or ventricular fibrillation
Associated with syncope and sudden death
Caused by a gain-of-function mutation in cardiac potassium channels
Sinus node dysfunction
Sinus arrest
Sinoatrial block
Sick sinus syndrome
Atrioventricular block
First degree
Second degree
Third degree

text: Gastroschisis
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Definition
Gastro means GIT tract, schisis means splitting or separating
Gastroschisis is a congenital abdominal wall defect, there is a full thickness hole in the abdominal wall at which the infant’s abdominal organs herniate
the hole mostly located on the right of the umbilicus
Definition
herniated organs has no cover, they have direct contact with external environment
Most commonly organs herniating through this hole are intestine, stomach and liver
Must be differentiated from omphalocele (this is explained a little bit later in the gastroschisis vs omphalocele chapter of this video)
Epidemiology
Gastroschisis incidence is 1 in 2500 live births and it is increasing every decade
10% of cases are associated with anomalies outside GI tract
Epidemiology
Gastroschisis infants have high risk of intrauterine growth restriction 60% thus greater risk for preterm labor too
Risk of preterm delivery in gastroschisis 25% in comparison with normal babies 5%
Gastroschises survival rate is 90% with treatment, 0% without treatment
Pathophysiology
Pathophysiology of gastroschisis is related to embryonic folding
Embryonic folding is the process by which the fetus converts from flat sheet of cells, into a tube like structure and it start at 4 weeks
Embryonic folding has to be complete for the abdominal wall to close , if not then gastroschisis occurs
OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Pathophysiology

This is caused by inadequate blood supply due to right umbilical artery premature regression (normally right umbilical artery stays longer until it regress while in gastroschisis it regress prematurely)
So there is not enough blood going to the abdominal wall and this lead to Gastroschisis which is hole in the right side of the abdominal wall that allows intestine to protrude through it
Intestine get irritated and inflamed when exposed to amniotic fluid
Pathophysiology
This lead to reduced bowel motility and absorption because of the irritation
Herniated bowel may have compromised vascular supply which lead to impaired bowel development
Complications: Intestinal stenosis, short bowel, intestinal atresia, perforation, necrosis, volvulus or GIT infections can occur
Causes
Cause unknown
But there is risk factors
Risk factors
Young maternal age < 20 years
Maternal low body mass index
Maternal use of salicylates like aspirin
Maternal genitourinary infection during first trimester
Maternal cigarette smoking or alcohol or illicit drug use
Gross appearance
Defect to the right of the umbilical cord insertion site, smooth edges and it is usually less than 4 cm in diameter
The defect is separated from the base of umbilical cord by small bridge of skin
Intestine are thickened with no overlying membrane
Gastroschisis vs omphalocele
Omphalocele is when the intestine protrudes into the umbilical cord and it stay sealed by the umbilical cord which protect it from the amniotic fluid while in gastroschisis there is no cover
Variants of gastroschisis
Closed or vanishing gastroschisis: abdominal wall defect has closed before birth => blood supply to the herniated bowel is impaired now => herniated bowel is now ischemic and necrosis occur
Left sided gastroschisis (rare): the only difference is that the defect is to the left of the umbilicus
Diagnosis

Gastroschisis can be diagnosed at the end of the first trimester by ultrasound, because the physiological return of intestine should be complete by 11 weeks of gestation if not then it is gastroschisis
US shows multiple loops of bowel floating freely in the amniotic fluid, bowel herniation is seen on the right of the umbilical cord insertion
Diagnosis
Gastroschisis can be differentiated from omphalocele by US too, in gastroschisis there is lack of membranous covering of the bowel
In Omphalocele there is high probability of CVS, and genitourinary anomalies while in Gastroschisis there is low probability for GIT, CNS, CVS, MSK and genitourinary anomalies
Some of those anomalies can be identified by US too
Diagnosis
Injury to the herniated bowel from exposure to the amniotic fluid or contracture of the umbilical ring is common

The injury also can be identified by US, features include: dilatation of the bowel, loss of peristaltic activity, changes in bowel wall echogenicity, alterations in mesenteric blood flow and changes in stomach position
Maternal alpha fetoprotein levels are elevated too
Delivery of gastroschisis baby
Vaginal delivery is possible with all gastroschisis cases unless the liver is herniated then C section delivery has to be done
Resuscitation
After delivery of gastroschisis newborn, ventilation or intubation might be needed
NG decompression tube should be inserted and IV access obtained
If there is bowel congestion, try to look for any kinking and relieve by repositioning of the bowel
Resuscitation
Bolus IV normal saline 20 ml/kg after delivery is obligatory to substitute the third space fluid loss and insensible fluid losses, sometimes 80 ml/kg is needed initially
Initial dose of ampicillin and gentamicin shortly after delivery to prevent GIT infections
Parenteral nutrition is very important in gastroschisis and should be used until bowel function goes back to normal
Treatment
The goal is to return the intestine back to the abdominal cavity and slowly introduce feeding to the baby
The two main options of treatment are
primary closure
staged closure with the use of a temporary silo and progressive reduction

Silo is a clear, sterile plastic or silicone bag that is placed over the exposed organs for putting pressure for gradual reduction and also the silo is effective in protection and preventing fluid loss
Primary closure
this procedure include reduction of the bowel back to the abdominal cavity and closing the defect
This procedure done quickly after birth as an attempt to return the herniated organs back to their place, if failed then silo method is done
Primary closure
Failure of primary closure is when
Intestine can’t be placed back into the abdominal cavity (not enough space)
Intestine can be placed but the intraabdominal pressure is higher than 10mmHg
Central venous pressure is greater than 4 mmHg when bowel placed back
Staged closure using silo
This method developed in the 1990s
This method start by applying silo (plastic or silicon bag) in the delivery room, after application the bowel is reduced gradually back into the abdominal cavity
Silo positioned around the opening without the need for sutures or anesthesia
Adewale O. Oyinloye1*, Auwal M. Abubakar1, Samuel Wabada2 and Lateef O. Oyebanji1, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Staged closure using silo
Bowel viability is assessed continuously while in silo to ensure no impairment in the blood supply
This process takes between 1 and 14 days until bowel is reduced, and then definitive closure is done which is similar to the primary closure
Intestinal atresia
Sometimes gastroschisis is associated with intestinal atresia
Intestinal atresia has to be anastomosed again
Post operative care

Ensure there are no effects from increased abdominal pressure (e.g. abnormal ventilation, decreased renal function, GIT ischemia), if abdominal compartment syndrome is suspected then laparotomy and silo placement should be performed
In Gastroschisis bowel function is decreased (motility and absorption are affected), and it gradually improves in most patients
Post operative care
No enteral feeding in gastroschisis until bowel function returns, during that time NG decompression, parenteral nutrition are required
When bowel activity returns, enteral feeding started gradually until enteral feeding is enough and that is when the patient can be discharged, this can take from 1 to 2 months

text: Omphalocele
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Definition
Omphalocele is a congenital abdominal wall defect, in which the abdominal viscera is herniating through the umbilical cord outside meaning the viscera will be covered by a sac (umbilical cord lining)
The location of the omphalocele defect could be mid abdominal, hypogastric or epigastric
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Definition
Omphalocele sac is comprised of an inner peritoneal layer and an outer amnion layer with Wharton’s jelly in between
Most commonly organs herniating are intestine, stomach and liver
Epidemiology
Omphalocele incidence is around 1 in 1500 in 14-18 weeks of gestation and 1 in 5000 at birth (most of omphalocele cases discovered early will be spontaneously lost or the pregnancy is terminated)
Incidence of omphalocele remained stable in comparison with gastroschisis incidence which is increasing
Epidemiology
Omphalocele has relatively high incidence of other congenital anomalies by 50-70% of the cases, these include:
Cardiac anomalies
GIT anomalies
Exstrophy of the bladder
Neural tube defects
Lung hypoplasia
Omphalocele can be associated with several syndromes including:
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
Pentalogy of Cantrell
Trisomies 13, 18 and 21
Beckwith- Weideman Syndrome
Omphalocele
Macroglossia
Organomegaly
Hypoglycemia
increased risk of Wilms tumor, hepatoblastoma and neuroblastoma in the future
Sydney S. Gellis and Murray Feingold, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Pentalogy of Cantrell
Omphalocele
Diaphragmatic hernia
Cardiac anomalies
Pericardial defect
Sternal cleft
Pathophysiology
Pathophysiology of omphalocele is related to embryonic folding
Embryonic folding is the process by which the fetus converts from flat sheet of cells, into a tube like structure and it start at 4 weeks
Embryonic folding has to be complete for the abdominal wall to close , if not then omphalocele develops
OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Pathophysiology

If the deficit in the embryonic folding process was related to the cranial fold then the omphalocele would be associated with other cranial fold defects like diaphragmatic hernia, cardiac anomalies, pericardial defect and sternal cleft
if the deficit is related to caudal fold then omphalocele might be associated with bladder exstrophy
Causes
Cause unknown
But there is risk factors
Risk factors
Genetic predisposition and chromosomal abnormalities
Maternal age of 35 years and older
Maternal use of salicylates like aspirin
Maternal diabetes
Maternal cigarette smoking or alcohol or illicit drug use
Diagnosis
Omphalocele can be diagnosed by routine two dimensional US evaluation by 18 weeks of gestation, first trimester detection is possible only with three dimensional US
Elevation of maternal serum AFP present in most cases same with gastroschisis
Diagnosis
Gastroschisis can be differentiated from omphalocele by US too, in gastroschisis there is lack of membranous covering of the bowel

In Omphalocele there is high probability of CVS, CNS and genitourinary anomalies, 70% of these anomalies can be detected by US thus knowing the survival rate (survival rate is highly hindered by cardiac anomalies), in comparison to Gastroschisis there is low probability for GIT, CNS, CVS, MSK and genitourinary anomalies
Delivery of Omphalocele baby
The goal is to deliver omphalocele patient as close to term as possible to maximize fetal growth and lung development
Spontaneous vaginal delivery is the preferred since C section has not shown any advantage
BUT many neonates with giant omphaloceles continue to be delivered by C section in many centers worldwide
Resuscitation
After delivery of omphalocele newborn, ventilation or intubation might be needed
Blood glucose is checked immediately and Dextrose might be given if it was low (Beckwith Wiedemann syndrome)
NG decompression tube should be inserted and IV access obtained
Resuscitation
Thorough search for associated anomalies is important, chest x ray looking for elongated thorax (pulmonary hypoplasia) and echocardiography looking for cardiac anomalies
The sac should be covered with saline soaked gauze and dressed to minimize fluid losses
Bolus IV normal saline 20 ml/kg after delivery might be needed to substitute the third space fluid loss and insensible fluid losses, fluid and temperature losses are much less than with gastroschisis
Resuscitation
Initial dose of ampicillin and gentamicin shortly after delivery to prevent GIT infections
Parenteral nutrition is very important in omphalocele and should be used until bowel function goes back to normal
Risk assessment
Risk assessed based on presence of associated anomalies
Isolated omphalocele (no associated anomalies) has the best survival of 90%, presence of associated anomalies decreases survival
Omphalocele can be classified into hypogastric, central and epigastric
Epigastric has the worst survival rate because of the presence of cardiac anomalies
Treatment
Treatment is with surgery goal is to return the intestine back to the abdominal cavity and slowly introduce feeding to the baby
Treatment options depend on the size of the omphalocele, baby’s gestational age and presence of associated comorbidities like respiratory insufficiency and associated anomalies
Treatment options
Primary closure of the defect: used in small omphaloceles (< 3 cm)
Delayed closure: used when the patient has giant omphalocele or has small omphalocele with associated comorbidities
Staged closure: used in patients with large defects and no associated comorbidities
Primary closure
Immediate primary closure consist of excision of the omphalocele sac, reduction of its content, umbilical cord is dissected and ligated and closure of the fascia and skin over the abdominal contents
Primary closure used in small defects < 3 cm in diameter
Larger defects that are easy to close (in case of minimal loss in abdominal domain) also can be treated by primary closure in the first month of life
Delayed closure
Used when the patient has giant omphalocele or has small omphalocele with associated comorbidities
This method include:
Umbilical cord is ligated and excised
the defect is then dressed daily with topical sulfasalazine non adherent dressing
with time the amnion become epithelized and the defect size decreases
In around 1 year when comorbidities have improved and the defect size decreased then definitive closure can be performed
Staged closure
Used in patients with large defects and no associated comorbidities
When there is significant loss of domain in the abdominal cavity, primary closure is not possible (lead to abdominal compartment syndrome), and that is when the staged closure comes in context
Staged closure is done using amniotic sac inversion technique
Staged closure
All of the amnion inversion procedure is done extraperitoneal and there is less risk of future adhesions and intestinal obstruction with this method
The amnion is inverted by attaching a silastic silo to the amnion-skin junction using sutures
The bowel and liver are progressively reduced  into the abdomen, the intraabdominal pressure is monitored using NG tube (should not exceed 20 mmHg) to prevent abdominal compartment syndrome
Staged closure
Reduction progresses on a daily basis until the contents lays flat and that is when the silo is removed

then the amnion is pulled and detachment of intestine is done from the amnion then it is inverted back and the edges are approximated and this process is repeated multiple times until simulated totoal closure of the abdominal wall is possible
Finally, The amnion is everted and dissected and abdomen is closed
Complications
Early complications include
Pulmonary hypoplasia and chronic lung disease and those are due to omphalocele disease process,
Cholestasis, sepsis, developmental delay, hypotonia, respiratory insufficiency, renal failure and abdominal compartment syndrome and those come as a result from the treatment
Late complications include hernia and GERD due to increase abdominal pressure

There is no role for blood urea nitrogen or e GFR in the diagnosis of AKI

text: Serum Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG)
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Subhaschandra Singh, Y. Sobita Devi, Shweta Bhalothia and Dr. Veeraraghavan Gunasekaran, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
SAAG
It is one of the investigations used to evaluate newly diagnosed or worsening ascites
It is used to distinguish the causes of ascites whether it is caused by portal hypertension or malignancy or other causes
Sample of the ascitic fluid is taken via paracentesis
Cancer Research UK, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
SAAG
And then the sample taken to laboratory to calculate albumin level and also sample of patient blood also taken for albumin level calculation
Then SAAG = serum albumin – ascites albumin
SAAG
If SAAG > 1.1 g/dL
Means the albumin level in blood is much higher than the ascitic fluid
This means that the ascitic fluid is forming due to high pressure driving the fluid into the peritoneum (from the vessels into peritoneum)
This high pressure is caused by portal hypertension
Portal hypertension is caused by: liver cirrhosis, heart failure, Budd Chiari syndrome …
SAAG
If SAAG < 1.1 g/dL
Means the albumin level in blood is little higher than the ascitic fluid
Here the problem is in the vessels, they are leaking the albumin and the fluid into the peritoneum
Causes: malignancy, infections, pancreatitis …
Total ascitic protein
Total protein of the ascitic fluid is used with the SAAG to identify the cause of ascites
Same ascites sample taken for SAAG is used to calculate total protein
Total ascitic protein
If total ascitic protein < 2.5 g/dL
Total ascitic protein is low
Mostly due to portal hypertension, other causes include nephrotic syndrome and tuberculosis peritonitis
Total ascitic protein
If total ascitic protein > 2.5 g/dL
Total ascitic protein is high
Causes include: heart failure, malignancy
SAAG
Total protein
Nephrotic syndrome
Liver cirrhosis, Budd Chiari syndrome
Cancer, pancreatitis, infection
Heart failure, veno occlusive disease

text: Spinal Cord Injury Classification According to ASIA
Sheldahl, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
DocSumomo, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Spinal cord injury classification
ASIA classification of spinal cord injury is the gold standard nowadays to classify these injuries
To classify spinal cord injury according to American spinal injury association, neurological examination has to be done looking for sensory or motor deficits
Motor examination is done using muscle power of the key muscles only looking for any motor deficits
Sensory examination is done using superficial modality (pinprick) and deep modality (touch) only looking for any deficits
Key muscles
C5
Elbow flexors
C6
Wrist extensors
C7
Elbow extensors
C8
Finger flexors
T1
5th finger abductors
L2
Hip flexors
L3
Knee extensors
L4
Ankle dorsiflexors
L5
Big toe extensors
S1
Ankle plantar flexors
Neurological examination
Muscle power is graded out of 5 according to the MRC grading
0/5: no muscle movement
1/5: visible muscle movement but with no movement at the joint
2/5: movement at the joint but not against gravity
3/5: movement against gravity, but not against added resistance
4/5: movement against resistance, but less than normal
5/5: normal power
Sensory is graded out of 2 according to
0: absent sensation
1: altered
2: normal
Classify by following these steps
Determine the sensory levels for right and left sides (each side graded independently), intact dermatome must be responding to pinprick and light touch sensation

Determine the motor levels for right and left sides (each side graded independently), motor level defined by the lowest key muscle (on the body) with grade 3 power and the muscles above this muscle are grade 5 power
Classify by following these steps

Determine the neurological level of injury: NLI refers to the lowest segment with intact sensation and motor function (grade 3 muscle power), NLI is the lower level of the sensory and motor levels assigned in step 1 and 2

Determine if the injury is complete or incomplete: if patient can’t voluntarily contract anal sphincter and sensory exam of S4, S5 is 0 and deep anal pressure is negative then injury is complete, otherwise injury is incomplete
Classify by following these steps
Now you can determine the injury grade according to ASIA impairment scale
ASIA impairment scale (AIS)
Grade
Description
A
Complete: no sensory or motor at S4-5
B

Sensory incomplete: sensory is preserved below neurological level of injury including sensation at S4-5, but motor function is preserved only to three levels below the motor level on either side of the body
C

Motor incomplete: motor is preserved at the S4-5 or the patient sensory is preserved at S4-5 with preservation of more than 3 motor levels below the level of injury (less than half key muscles below level of injury have muscle power equals to 3 or more)
D
Motor incomplete: same as AIS C with more than half of the key muscles below level of injury have muscle power grade of 3 or more
E
Normal

text: Spinal Cord Injury Classification According to ASIA
Sheldahl, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
DocSumomo, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Spinal cord injury classification
ASIA classification of spinal cord injury is the gold standard nowadays to classify these injuries
To classify spinal cord injury according to American spinal injury association, neurological examination has to be done looking for sensory or motor deficits
Motor examination is done using muscle power of the key muscles only looking for any motor deficits
Sensory examination is done using superficial modality (pinprick) and deep modality (touch) only looking for any deficits
Key muscles
C5
Elbow flexors
C6
Wrist extensors
C7
Elbow extensors
C8
Finger flexors
T1
5th finger abductors
L2
Hip flexors
L3
Knee extensors
L4
Ankle dorsiflexors
L5
Big toe extensors
S1
Ankle plantar flexors
Neurological examination
Muscle power is graded out of 5 according to the MRC grading
0/5: no muscle movement
1/5: visible muscle movement but with no movement at the joint
2/5: movement at the joint but not against gravity
3/5: movement against gravity, but not against added resistance
4/5: movement against resistance, but less than normal
5/5: normal power
Sensory is graded out of 2 according to
0: absent sensation
1: altered
2: normal
Classify by following these steps
Determine the sensory levels for right and left sides (each side graded independently), intact dermatome must be responding to pinprick and light touch sensation

Determine the motor levels for right and left sides (each side graded independently), motor level defined by the lowest key muscle (on the body) with grade 3 power and the muscles above this muscle are grade 5 power
Classify by following these steps

Determine the neurological level of injury: NLI refers to the lowest segment with intact sensation and motor function (grade 3 muscle power), NLI is the lower level of the sensory and motor levels assigned in step 1 and 2

Determine if the injury is complete or incomplete: if patient can’t voluntarily contract anal sphincter and sensory exam of S4, S5 is 0 and deep anal pressure is negative then injury is complete, otherwise injury is incomplete
Classify by following these steps
Now you can determine the injury grade according to ASIA impairment scale
ASIA impairment scale (AIS)
Grade
Description
A
Complete: no sensory or motor at S4-5
B

Sensory incomplete: sensory is preserved below neurological level of injury including sensation at S4-5, but motor function is preserved only to three levels below the motor level on either side of the body
C

Motor incomplete: motor is preserved at the S4-5 or the patient sensory is preserved at S4-5 with preservation of more than 3 motor levels below the level of injury (less than half key muscles below level of injury have muscle power equals to 3 or more)
D
Motor incomplete: same as AIS C with more than half of the key muscles below level of injury have muscle power grade of 3 or more
E
Normal

It is one of the investigations used to evaluate newly diagnosed or worsening ascites
It is used to distinguish the causes of ascites whether it is caused by portal hypertension or malignancy or other causes
Sample of the ascitic fluid is taken via paracentesis
Cancer Research UK, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

If SAAG < 1.1 g/dL
Means the albumin level in blood is little higher than the ascitic fluid
Here the problem is in the vessels, they are leaking the albumin and the fluid into the peritoneum
Causes: malignancy, infections, pancreatitis …

Mostly due to portal hypertension, other causes include nephrotic syndrome and tuberculosis peritonitis

Causes include: heart failure, malignancy

Overview
SIADH and DI are both disorders affecting the ADH secretion
ADH hormone secreted from pituitary gland and work on the V2 receptor in the collecting duct to absorb more water from the duct into the circulation

Overview
Diabetes insipidus is deficiency or inadequacy of ADH secretion leading to decrease water absorption from collecting duct, thus leading to polyuria and polydipsia
DI on two types: nephrogenic (the V2 receptors doesn’t work), or central (the pituitary doesn’t secrete ADH)

Next, The Key Differences Between the Two Conditions Will Be Explained:

SIADH caused by:
Tumors secreting ADH such as lung cancer
Head injuries
Medications
Any disease affecting pituitary gland or hypothalamus
DI caused by:
Central caused by head trauma, tumors affecting pituitary or hypothalamus
Nephrogenic could be genetic or acquired due to kidney disorders or medications
Presentation
SIADH present with nausea, vomiting, malaise, headache, lethargy and seizures from the cerebral edema caused by hyponatremia
Diabetes insipidus present with polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration and seizures
Urine output
SIADH: urine output reduced and urine is concentrated because body is absorbing more water from the urine
DI: urine output is increased and urine is diluted because body losing more water
Thirst
In SIADH, patients doesn’t feel thirsty as much as normal because they are retaining water
In DI, patients feel extremely thirsty and drink a lot of water because they are losing water
Serum sodium levels
SIADH lead to dilutional hyponatremia (low sodium because of the excessive water in circulation)
DI: normal or high sodium levels
Treatment
SIADH: treat the cause and restrict fluid intake to prevent further load on circulation
DI: treat according to the type and cause, and increase fluid intake

text: Portal hypertension

Contents
Overview
Pathophysiology
Causes
Clinical features
Diagnosis
Treatment
Overview
Portal hypertension is increased pressure within the portal venous system
Pressure difference of 6 mmHg or more between the portal vein and the inferior vena cava confirms portal hypertension diagnosis
Liver cirrhosis is the most common cause for portal hypertension
Pathophysiology
Portal vein collects blood from bowel and go through the liver and into the hepatic vein and then to inferior vena cava
OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Pathophysiology
Portal hypertension develops when the resistance to the portal blood flow increases leading to increase the pressure difference between portal and inferior vena cava

Resistance could be in the liver in form of cirrhosis, or it could be prehepatic in the portal vein in form of portal vein thrombosis, or it could be post hepatic like Budd Chiari syndrome (occlusion of the hepatic vein)
Pathophysiology

When the portal blood pressure remains elevated, body tries to decrease this pressure by opening the collateral vessels that bypass the liver’s normal circulation (thus bypassing the resistance), examples of the collaterals include:
Esophageal varices
Gastric varices
Rectal varices
Periumbilical veins (caput medusa)
Splenic collaterals
Retroperitoneal collaterals
Causes
Prehepatic: portal vein thrombosis, arteriovenous malformations or fistulas involving the portal vein
Intrahepatic: congenital hepatic fibrosis, schistosomiasis, liver cirrhosis, veno-occlusive disease
Post hepatic: Budd-Chiari syndrome, inferior vena cava obstruction, constrictive pericarditis
Clinical features
No symptoms until complications arise

Cirrhosis is the most common cause of portal hypertension and when patient have it, they present with jaundice, palmar erythema, spider nevi, gynecomastia, ascites, asterixis and hepatic encephalopathy
Patient might present with hematemesis or melena from bleeding varices
Clinical features
Splenomegaly is reliable sign in the diagnosis of portal hypertension, if no splenomegaly think of other differential diagnosis
Diagnosis
CBC to look for anemia from bleeding, thrombocytopenia from bleeding or liver failure
LFT, RFT looking for liver or renal failure
Coagulation profile to look for deficiencies in the coagulation factors from liver failure
Diagnosis
Doppler US of the portal vein looking for stenosis or thrombosis
Abdominal US looking for liver cirrhosis, ascites and splenomegaly
Endoscopy looking for varices
Diagnosis
Patient with ascites need paracentesis to look for the cause
Measurement of portal pressure often not required to make the diagnosis because the clinical features are enough
Treatment
Treat the cause: e.g. portal vein thrombosis treated with anticoagulation, liver cirrhosis treated with liver transplantation
Treat the complications: e.g. hematemesis treated with supportive measures (blood transfusions…) and endoscopic therapy
Empiric antibiotics for prophylaxis against SBP
Ascites treated with sodium restriction, diuretics and paracentesis

text: We have four generations of the penicillin antibiotics

First generation represented by the benzyl penicillin (penicillin G) which is the original penicillin discovered by Alexander Fleming and its modifications which include procaine penicillin, benzathine penicillin, penicillin V.
Second generation is called the anti staphylococci Penicillin (also called beta lactamase resistant penicillin); Includes Methicillin, cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, floxacillin, nafcillin
Third generation is called the amino Penicillin (also called extended spectrum penicillin); includes ampicillin and amoxicillin
Fourth generation is the anti pseudomonal Penicillin; includes ticarcillin, azlocillin, mezlocillin and piperacillin

Overview
it is called infectious mononucleosis because infectious means the disease can spread to other people, mononucleosis because there is increase in mononuclear cells count (reactive lymphocytes
It is also called glandular fever and kissing disease
Glandular because it is associated with swollen lymph nodes
Kissing because it spread through saliva
Overview

It is primarily spread through saliva but can rarely be spread through semen or blood. Incubation period is about 4 weeks and infected people spread the disease during this period before symptoms develop
IM not highly contagious thus isolation of cases is not necessary
Presentation
Fever which resolves after 2 weeks
Pharyngitis: with tonsillar exudates
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

lymphadenopathy: non tender cervical anterior and posterior, inguinal and axillary lymphadenopathy

Presentation
Splenomegaly
Palatal petechiae
Periorbital edema
Fatigue
Presentation
Death is rare but can occur due to respiratory obstruction, hemorrhage from splenic rupture, thrombopenia and encephalitis
In children under 10 years disease is mild, in adults over 30 disease is severe and prlonoged
Causes
Epstein Barr virus: about 90% of cases of IM are caused by that
Cytomegalovirus: 5-7% of cases
Pathophysiology
Virus replicates in epithelial cells in the pharynx leading to pharyngitis
Virus infect B cells through CD21 => the body respond to this by activating the cytotoxic T cells which attack the infected B cells resulting in enlarged atypical lymphocytes (downey cells)
Diagnosis
Medical history: Highest risk in ages 10-30, close contact with other infected people, fever and sore throat
Physical examination by lymph node examination looking for enlargement , and abdominal examination looking for enlarged spleen
Heterophile antibody test (AKA mononuclear spot test is positive in IM
Differential diagnosis

Acute cytomegalovirus infection and toxoplasmosis present with similar symptoms as IM but differentiated using Heterophile antibody test which will be negative in both of these conditions and positive in IM
Treatment
Self limiting
Symptomatic treatment
Avoid contact sports and weight training to decrease the risk of splenic rupture (because some cases of IM there would be splenic enlargement)

Overview
Skin grafting or flapping is a type of surgery involves transplantation of skin from the donor site to the recipient site.
Grafting or flapping used in
Extensive wound or trauma
Burns
Areas of extensive skin loss due to infection
Surgeries require skin replacement like removal of skin cancers
Skin graft
Skin graft consist of epidermis and some portion of the dermis that is removed from its blood supply and transferred to another location

Skin graft uses

Control infection

Skin graft types
Autograft => same person
Allograft (homograft) => from different human
Xenograft (heterograft) => from different species
Graft types according to thickness

Full thickness skin grafts contain epidermis and entire dermis with its elastic fibers => full thickness skin graft have elastic properties and primary contracture which make it good for replacing the sites that need elasticity like anterior elbow joint skin
Partial thickness skin grafts contain epidermis and varying thickness of the dermis and it is associated with secondary contracture
Primary contracture vs secondary contracture of skin graft

Primary contracture is the immediate recoil of freshly harvested grafts as a result of the elastin in the dermis, the more the thickness the more the dermis the more the primary contracture, primary contracture is the good types of contracture making graft more elastic

Secondary contracture involve the contracture of the healed graft due to myofibroblast activity and it is more in the split thickness grafts. Secondary contracture is bad making the graft more prone to hypertrophic scarring

Survival of skin graft depends on the ability of the graft to receive nutrients through revascularization. Revascularization of skin graft occurs in three phases:

Serum imbibition phase which last for the first 24 hours after grafting. when graft placed into the recipient bed binding the graft to the bed, absorption of nutrients into the graft occurs by capillary action from the recipient bed
Survival of skin graft
Inosculation phase for the second 24 hours after grafting. In which vascular network is established between the cut vessels on the underside of the skin graft and the capillary beds in the wound bed
Revascularization phase: in the third 24 hours after grafting. the graft is revascularized through kissing of the capillaries that are already formed in phase 2

hematoma under graft => elevation of graft and no kissing of blood vessels
infection
inadequate immobilization => like in anterior elbow you want to put back slap to immobilize elbow for success of graft

Misevaluation of the wound => in bed with poor blood supply or infection
Dependent  position

Regional flaps from same region as the defect like in arm or hand

Flaps are classified according to blood supply into axial flaps and random flaps:

Axial flap: there is a well named artery in the pedicle of the flap
island flap

free flap

Mixed
