text: Nephrotic Syndrome
CharlesPicavet, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Polarlys, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons
Overview
Normally, protein molecules shouldn’t be lost in urine in concentrations higher than 150 mg per day
If the urine protein excretion exceeds 150 mg per day then this is called proteinuria and it is caused by many diseases including UTI, nephrotic syndrome, CKD…
When the urine protein become > 3.5 g per day then it is called nephrotic range proteinuria and it is caused by nephrotic syndrome
Cause
In nephrotic syndrome the kidney glomerulus would have some kind of problem that make it pass protein molecules into the urine, the problem exactly in the podocyte (NephrOtic = POdocyte)
Artwork by Holly Fischer, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Pathophysiology
Due to the albumin lost in urine, liver tries to compensate by increasing albumin synthesis but it fails to reach the normal albumin levels
As a result of the protein lost in urine, the oncotic pressure decreases which stimulate the hepatic lipoprotein synthesis which lead to hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia
Lipid become entrapped in casts and enclosed by the plasma membrane of a degenerative renal tubular cells which lead to oval fat body in urine
Presentation
Frothy urine
Polarlys, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons
Presentation
Edema
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Presentation
Hypertension
Steven Fruitsmaak, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Presentation
Hyperlipidemia (serum cholesterol > 300)
Proteinuria (3.5 g/day)
Hypoalbuminemia
Mark-shea at English Wikipedia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Presentation
Anemia because transferrin is also lost in urine
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Presentation
Increase risk of infection
Increased risk of thrombosis
Diagnosis
Best initial test is urinalysis which detect protein lost in urine, and any urinary casts
24 hour urine protein test
Normal protein excretion < 150 mg/day
Nephrotic range > 3.5 g/day
Urine protein to creatinine ratio
Easier to obtain than 24 hours urine collection
Diagnosis
Comprehensive metabolic panel looking for hypoalbuminemia (normal albumin= 3.5-5 g/dl)
Renal function test: blood urea nitrogen and creatinine
Serum electrolytes and lipid profile looking for any changes
Confirmatory test is renal biopsy looking for the exact pathology
Treatment
Curative treatment
Treat the cause usually with immunosuppressive therapy
Supportive treatment
Strict blood pressure control < 130/80 mmHg using ACEs or ARBs
Hyperlipidemia treated with statins
Edema treated with sodium restriction and diuretics
Thrombophilia treated with anticoagulation
Infections treated with antibiotics
Complications
Thrombosis
Thrombosis typically seen in > 10g of proteinuria
Coagulation and anti coagulation factors are lost into the urine including anti thrombin III factor
Complications
Thrombosis
Liver tries to compensate for that by making more pro coagulation factors which make the problem worse
Volume depletion from diuretic therapy and reduced oncotic pressure lead to hemoconcentration and increased PLT aggregation which lead to thrombus formation and thrombosis
Complications
Infection
Immunoglobulins lost in urine
Patient become more susceptible to infections mostly with staphylococci and streptococci bacteria
Complications
Acute renal failure Due to hypovolemia (fluid shifted from intravascular into tissues = edema)
Pulmonary edema
Growth retardation
Etiology
Primary glomerular diseases include immune mediated injury to the podocytes
Minimal change disease
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Membranous nephropathy
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Etiology
Secondary glomerular diseases includes systemic diseases that also affect the glomerulus
Amyloidosis
Diabetic nephropathy
Systemic lupus erythematosus (lupus nephritis)

Overview
One of the primary glomerular diseases that lead to nephrotic syndrome

MCD is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, it accounts for 90% of nephrotic syndrome cases in children younger than 5y and 50% of nephrotic syndrome cases in children older than 10y
MCD accounts for 10-15% of nephrotic syndrome cases in adults

Secondary

Immune attack initiated by T cells against the podocytes for unknown reason
T cells injuries the podocyte foot processes leading to effacement of these foot processes and subsequently nephrotic syndrome

Elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels and thrombocytosis are usually found in MCD patients during relapse as result of plasma volume contraction
Confirmatory test is renal biopsy

Children younger than 10 presenting with idiopathic nephrotic syndrome: biopsy is not indicated, you treat them like they have minimal change disease
Children younger than 10 presenting with features does not go with minimal change disease like gross hematuria, renal dysfunction then renal biopsy is indicated
Children older than 10 and Adults: renal biopsy is indicated to establish diagnosis

MCD responds very well to corticosteroids
Corticosteroids are used in high doses for 12-16 weeks then tapered over 6 months

Terminology
Focal means when doing a biopsy there is less than 50% of glomeruli involved
Segmental means portion of the glomerulus is involved, others are normal
Glomerulosclerosis: sclerosis means scar
So it means less than 50% of glomeruli are scarred
Overview
FSGS is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults (in children most common cause of nephrotic syndrome is the MCD)
FSGS is second most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children
FSGS is common in people of west African descent (the primary genetic type)
Overview
FSGS famous for causing damage to transplanted kidney in less than 24 hours
Minimal change disease and FSGS on the same spectrum of podocyte injury (both affect foot processes): MCD is mild injury, FSGS is severe
Poor prognosis
Etiology
Primary FSGS:
idiopathic
Genetic/ familial
Secondary FSGS
HIV
Sickle cell anemia
Drugs (pamidronate, heroin)
Massive obesity
Renal injury (e.g. renal injury from HUS)
Systemic disease
Pathogenesis
In primary FSGS there is injury to the podocyte due to a circulating toxin
Secondary FSGS
Reduced renal mass, sickle cell and obesity lead to increased glomerular capillary blood pressure lead to hyperfiltration through the glomerulus and subsequent podocyte injury
In HIV, drugs (heroin, pamidronate) there is a direct injury to the podocyte either by the virus or the drug
Renal biopsy
Light microscopy shows segmental sclerosis
Immunofluorescence shows deposition of C3 complement and IgM in area of the scar
Electron microscopy shows effacement of foot processes
Since FSGS is focal, the abnormality may not show on renal biopsy and it would be normal leading to initial diagnosis of MCD

text: MELD Score: model for end stage liver disease
This score used to predict mortality in patients with chronic liver disease and prioritize them for liver transplantation
Takes into account three lab values: serum bilirubin, serum Cr and INR
MELD = 3.78×ln[serum bilirubin (mg/dL)] + 11.2×ln[INR] + 9.57×ln[serum creatinine (mg/dL)] + 6.43
There is phone app that calculate it
The result mostly range from 6 to 40
The higher the score, the greater severity of liver dysfunction
